AR ignoramus is a spontaneous agnostic. LovE laughs even more heartily at logic than at 'ocksmitbs. A MAN'S eye may be cowardly when his nose is pugnacious. MANY a man who thinks he is thinking is merely digesting yesterday's newspaper. SEE: "Do you recollect the night you proposed to me? I bent my head aed didn't say anything." He: "Quite right, but you've made up for it since." CLARA : "I think I'll try on my new bathing dress this morning." Gertrude : "Why, you tried it on last night when it came." Clara: "That was on myself. To-day lam going to try it on— the men." AN HONEST CONFESSION.—" What do you find the most oiffluult task?" asked the idle friend. "The hardest thing about my job," the all-round clerk replied, "is going on with my work when I have drawn my pay in advance." TIIE CONCEIT OF MAN.—" What are you going to du with that blossom?' "1 am going to give it to the man I love to-night." "To-night? Non- sense ! Why uot give it to me now?" "Do you not regret the hours you spent in gloatisig over your hoarded coin?" asked the good old clergyman. "I do," said the hardened old miser, bitterly ; "I might have spent the time making more money." IN EXTENCATION.—Akins : "1 understand that Miss Oldangles whom young Whoopler married re- cently, is very wealthy ? " Grimshaw : " Oh, yes. There were extenuating circumstances." MRS. TLNSPOT : "1 am so glad that you are engaged to Harry Willoughby: Was it a long courtship?" Miss Skidmore : "Not very. My cyclometer registered about 700 miles." READY TO OBLIGE. —"Oh !" gasped Mrs. Timid, as she saw a man stealing her silver-ware; " it's a burglar !" "At your serviee, mum," politely returned the burglar. MORE DEADLY THAN SCALPING. Mamma : "Playing Indian is so rough. Why are you cry- ing ? Have they been scalping you again ?" Spotted Panther (alias Willie) : " No, mamma ; we have been smoking the pipe of peace." DIED WITH THE LICENCE.—" Hawkins received a notice from the Inland Revenue people the other day to come round and get a new licence for his dog, as the old permit had expired." "What did he do?" "He wrote back that so had the dog." " TRAMP : "I say, missile, are you the only one ID charge of this yer 'ouse ?" Farmer's wife : "Well, I'm almost alone. I've only got this dog and this revolver to help me. Do you want any- thing?" Tramp : " Nutthink, lidy, only this— there's a goodish many suspishus kerricters about just now. Good evenin', lidy." BENEnicr : I tell you old boy, you ought to get married. You don't know what comfort it is to know that you've got a wife at home to patch your clothes." Singleton: "That's all right, bus I prefer to stay single and not have my clothet patched." _ . .

ENVIED HIMSELF.—Judy : " Ah, Dinnis, it do be ehtrange to hear ye talkin' that way, whin it was yersilf that usted to be tillin' me that Oi was the shwatest craychure in the wurruld." Dinnie : "Did Oi iver till yez that, Judy?" Judy : "In- dada an' ye did, Dinnis 1" Dinnis : " Begorra, an' ef that's so, thin Oi. invy mesilf the condition Oi mnsht hey be'n in at the toime." His DEFINITION.—" What is a flirt?" asked the small boy. "A flirt," replied the old bachelor, "is a pretty woman." "But what kind of a pretty woman I" persisted the small boy. "Any kind of a pretty woman," answered the old bachelor. " Well, how pretty must she be!" the youngster insisted. "Oh, pretty enough to have a chance to flirt," returned the old bachelor, irritably. And still the boy was not satisfied ; but as he grows older he will understand it better. LIICK.—" The man who owns the farm next to mine is the luckiest fellow I ever saw." " What are you talking about? There's no such thing ae luck." "There isn't, hey? Then will you tell ME how it happened that he bored for water and struck oil, while I bored for oil andetruck water?' SEE: "Did you stay long in Venice?" He "Only a couple of days, but I saw everything worth seeing." She: " Really ! Then you saw the lion of St. Mark's, I suppose!" He : "Rather ! Saw him fed." (And the conversation flagged); "MAY I ask, ma'am," said the new boarder, "if this is imitation coffee?" "And may I ask why you ask?" queried the imperturbable land- lady. "Because real coffee, ma'am, keeps me awake nights." ' "By the exercise of a little patience, then," said the smiling landlady, "you will soon be able to answer the question for your. ? Won't you have another cup?" ARE you the society editor?" asked the large lady, who seemed to fill the room. "No, madam," said the seie addressed. "I am only the Court re- porter." " Rsally ! lam surprised. But, perhaps you will do. Your paper said in its account of the affair at my house that floral decorations 'lent beauty to the scene.' I wish you would have your paper state that the floral beauty was aot lent. Everything was paid for." His sister wished to discourage him, but was anxious to do it in a quiet way that would not make trouble—so she said: "How old is she?" was asked. "she says she is 18," he replied. " Well," she returned, "the next time you go to see her you'd better take along am almanac. She evidently has forgotten how to reckon time:" N.Vhen it comes to breaking things gently there is no one who is spite so successful as a disgusted woman. WHEN Mr. A. J. Balfour was Chief Secretary of 4 Ireland, 'ne one day came across a daughter of .4e•Erin digging up her patch of potatoes, and he K remarlik don their quality. " Ah, bad luck to Mr. Balfour I I wish I could see him !" said the woman. "The seeds he gave us were no good." "I'm Mr. Balfour." She gazed hard, and after a 'list with him, then exclaimed: "Sure, now, haven't I often heard that the devil's not so black lie he's painted " A Fueitearia Now then, my dear," said Mr. Binks, as he placed his camera in poeitiom compose yourself and let a pleasant thought pass through your mind." " Nice time to expect a woman to have pleasant thoughts, isn't it?" exclaimed Mrs. Binks. "The -boiler sprung a leek, the tire gone out, the bread settled fiat as a pancake, no firewood, pump won't pump a drop, baby's got a pain, the twins to dress for school, • music-teacher coming to give Emmeline her lesson, washerwoman soon be here, I should be at the station this motrens to meet mother, have just an • hour left before I'm due at the morning session to deliver my lecture before the Good Housekeeper's Club on the subject of 'How to Manage a Kitchen'; yes, it's a nice time for a pleasant thought to pass through a woman's mind.' ONLY A RECRUIT, BUT A DEAD SHOT.—A good story is told at the expense of a lieutenant who was drilling recruits in revolver practice. One of the recruits was a tall and ungainly fellow from a mountain district. The mountaineer was shown how to load, hold, and handle his pistol by the dapper young officer, and after many corrections by the officer finally struck the right way to hold the revolver. "is that right?" he asked, at last. "All right," responded the lieutenant. "Now see if you can fire without killing any of our men." Rip ! went the revolver, pointing towards a target one hundred yards distant. Ping, ping, ping! went the bullets until the six-shooter was empty. The target was brought in, and there were six clear bull's-eyes. "Is that right?" asked the raw.boned Southerner. The lieutenant did not say a word, and the camp has been laughing ever since. WHO SHE WAS The following story of a famous doctor is not a new one, but the point is a good one, though the doctor's speeen was blunt. Dr. Jephsen, an English physician of former repu- tation like Dr. Abernethy, won his fame partly by his bluntness. One day he was called to the Duchess of Marlborough, who told him of all her symptoms at great length. His advice was: "One egg and one cup of tea for breakfast; then a walk ; a piece of cold roast beef for luncheon; then a walk; a good cutlet for dinner; then another walk, and then to bed. No carriage riding." "You seem to forget who and what I am !" said the duchess. "Not at all," replied Dr. Jephsen. "You are an old woman with a rained stomach !" kiv DEAR NELLIE. The blouse is now worn, but is more for I on,e, and evening wear, as it is rarely cc., n without a skirt exactly matching ih colour, when it is prac- tically a complete costume. For those who wear black the blouse is invaluable, and it is useful with coat and skirt costumes, the blouse to serve as a bodice for home wear. There is a remarkable freshness about some of the latest hats. One is frankly as flat as a pancake, a mere eirclo, of straw before it is arranged, but in the milliner's hands it achieves shape, for it is sharply turtied up in front and the same at the back, so that the back and front meet, and is then trimmed at the back with a handful of flowers and a bold Low of ribbon. Another is the Spanish turban, as flat and as compact as a Toreador's, draped with and set with a very slight tilt. " .00 - r

Ruffles of all kinds continue to he greatly worn almost to the entire exclusion of the once general feather boa. What is perhaps the favourite type of ruffle beyond all others is of black net very closely and fully pleated, and reaching to the waist in front, where the ends are finished with bows of ribbon which are rather newer than the chenille fringes, or the streamers of velvet ribbon with metal tags. White tulle and point d'esprit ruffles are also in high favour, and very prettily do they enframe a young face. The very smartest of all the ruffles, however, are made of huge, silken poppies or roses, closely crushed, as it were, so as to form a thick rope, and finished with trails or streamers of tiny blossoms threaded together. Some of these ruffs are so huge that they must be worn well back on the shoulders and so form a sort of background of soft and fluffy quilling against which the wearer's head stands out in relief. Lace collars are nearly as popular as ever, but those of brown, ecru, or string-coloured, linen, with open-work ornamentations, have to some degree replaced the guipure and Renaissance lace collars of last season. On the fashionable glat.4 boleros, collars of white corded silk, edged with lace in ecru or string-colour, or with the equally novel muslin applique also in ecru, look exceed- ingly well, as do collars of white glace with a bor- dering of flat jet flowers sewn along the extre:ec edge.

A charming dress was made of very fine, glossy white cloth, and was made with a plain box-pleat in front, widening from the waist to the hem. The rest of the skirt is trimmed with a graduated, ' shaped flounce, arranged in flat pleats, which are- sewn down for half their length and allowed to fall out below. A thick silk ruching trims the skirt round the hem. The lace above the flounce is cream coloured. The bodice is slashed, showing creamy lace beneath. Lace motifs are on the yoke and sleeves, and the revere are faced with lace.: Pipings of black silk cord and tiny fano), buttons, arranged in groups of three, fasten the bodice. The collar and chemisette are made of transparent muslin very finely tucked. This dress would be admirable if carried out in white alpaca and cream-coloured lace; or in a grey canvas with slashes of creamy silk and pipings of black velvet.
I

A new style of skirt is tucked from the waist, and has a very narrow front breadth, over which the sides gores are stitched in such a way that a quarter-inch fold projects over the front breadth. This is practically a narrow tuck, and is in keep- ing with those which appear at the waist. The tucks begin as near the front breadth as possible, the first beiag nearly a quarter of a yard deep, the ninth and last little more than an inch. Voile is a capital material for making these tucked skirts, which, by the way, are often finished with a flounce, which is both shaped and tucked, and possibly also trimmed with fancy ribbon or velvet just over a quarter of an inch in width. Let me describe one of electric blue. The flounce was about a quarter of a yard deep when three narrow tucks had been made just above the half-inch hem. Two rows of narrow magpie velvet trimmed this flounce in a series of vandykes, deep enough almost to touch the tucks. Between each of these van- dykes five tiny tucks started from the top of the flounce and ran down for varying lengths, the centre tuck measuring four inches, the outside ones barely two. A pretty bolero is made partly of ivory-white lace and partly of watered silk in the same shade. The lace is of the kind that resembles rows of insertion sewn together, and the undersleeves are also made of it. The revers, in watered silk are edged round with a fine embroidery worked in silks, or the softest and thinnest muslin. The cuffs and the shaped belt are made of this em- broidery, which is in the faintest pastel flower tones. The oversleeves are in the watesed silk, finished with a few narrow tucks. The bands into which the sleeves are gathered at the wrists are also finely tucked. The vest is soft white muslin, falling from a horizontally-tucked yoke. Light as lace is, this kind of bolero is very useful for putting on with almost any skirt, and a pretty front. The addition gives at once a look of care and taste to an otherwise quiet toilette. Worn with a black skirt and a pink silk neck-band, it =ay prove very becoming. Your loving

The King, it seem. intends to revive golfing: as a Royal game, and his Majestyds having new golf linker completed in the grounds of Windsor Castle. lKing Edward has not hitherto taken muted interest in the game, though aa Prince of Woks, he became patron of the " Royal and Ancient " Golf Club of St Andrews, as far back as 1883. The game. in fact, has bad but little .favourjrom roa ally in modern ciao 5. Kiug hero s VI of Scotland was a great golf player, and as James I of England he established the first club in London, but since the: time of the Stuerts, it has not been a favourite pastime of the Royal family, and it is of course only in recent 'timed that the game has been played to any extent out of Scotland. Battle Abbey, the residence of the late and venerable Duchess of Cleveland, now passes under the win of the late Duke to Captain Ferster,his great nephew. It was purchased by the Duke of Cleveland from Sir Godfrey Webster, and the Duchess only held the property with a jointure of £20,C00 a sear, for her life Though she spent so much of her time in travelling, the Duchess was greatly attached to the place, and had it fitteel up in great splendour. No one who was permitted to see it was, except as a see cial fay ur, ever allowed to sketch there. In her book "The Battle Abbey Roll," the late Duchess gives us an interesting and historical account of Battle Abbey, which was founded by William the Conqueror to commemorate his victory over Harcld,and in canich he deposited the famous roll, containing Ch' names of all the leaders who accompanied him to this country. One is glad to read the appeal which is put forth by Lady Ebury in connection with the Soldiers and Sailors Help Society, 115 Ehury-street, Belgravia. The Society she says, has no difficulty in finding places for dis- charged men of good eharacter,but there are many men on the books who have been partially disabled in the war, but are quite able to undertake light work. It is on behalf of these men who have deserved well of the country, that Lady Ebery appeals to employers of labour. The state, which has a particular responsibility with regard to the men who have been wounded, might also do something in the matter, and might employ them in duties which could be discharged very well by a man who had lost say an eye or an arm in the war. Miss Violet Brooke-Hunt, who was speaking the other day at the meeting of the Women's Agricultural and Horticultural internatimal Union, referred to the open. ing3 for women workers in South Africa, and said that r a laundres. could make a fortune in Pretoria. All that would be wanted is a little capital and ability to man gp laavts native labour, which, of course, Is not without its pecu- Lairt v to taiteis. iS eatibw°eiethhaollwe so r 1 With the ability and of difficulties, should e think of going out to South Africa, for some time to come. Things are likely to remain very unsettled and to one should go out unless with slew settled plans or prospects. The United British Women's Emigration Ass e elation have recently established a South African Expansion Committee, whose special busineas it will be to aid women emigrants to find openings at the Cape. A new feature in the London season this year, has been the holding of a service in one or two of the more fashionable churches at nine o'clock on Sunday ever:- logs, at which a large proportion of the congregation, both men and women, attend in evening dress. Like the clergy who think is better that the Sunday cyclist, or boating man should attend in his flannels than star away, so this new experiment seems only influenced by the desire to adapt the service to the man era and custom% of society. Still it will no,doubt appear not a little skockiug to many with cld-fasbioned views. At the East end or London, ttere Is &Ise a new departure at some of the Churcnes, where open-air pulpits have been are cled,from which the ministers preach to those people in the crowded tboroughf ores who will not come inside., The skirt with the separate flounce, cut godet or circular fashion, still reigns supreme. Sometimes this is of equal depth back and fro nt,sometirnes low in front I and high behind, while occasionally it is divided into , three and four flounces, the lining only remaining in one. Evening skirts are,,if possiye, fuller than ever, from knee to hem, where they flow out in huge billows, And elaboration, alas, is still the order of be day. It l would often be all easier talk to enumerate those trim. mings not appearing on the gown fashionable, than those which have found a place thereon. Particularly restful, after the over elaborateness, of which we have all grown not a little weary, is the soft, clinging gown of purest white. worn by Miss Eva Moore in the last scene of The Wilderness —which by the way is quite the most delightful play of the season, In its stern, yet beautiful timplicity,—its only ornament consisting of a narrow belt of silver, which temps the waist—this gown stands out Very easily first among the many exquisite creaeions en evidence just now, at the St James's Theatre. Metal work from Psris and Berlin rivals the best our borne manufacturers can send out. Ignoring the trifles in " New Art " metal, there are everywhere chains, charms, ferrets, and tags, some oxidised, and tome gilt, and ell excellent in design. Into many, little atonee are introduced which sparkle out brightly now and then. In waist clasps again, there is much variety, the temptation to he avoided being that of choosing at one time, several trinkets, each of a different metal. Fooliah charms, misrepresenting animals, and ur- f , decorative Objects, are happily Yieldicg ground to really pretty items. Some of the newest represent a beartease and leaves, about as large as a shilling, enamelled in natural colours, on perforated geld-tinged metal. Tnis pretty cover shows flashes of brightness through the epeees of the design, these being given forth by a tiny tni.ror conecaled behind it. On pushing the hearteas.l aside with the finger, the wee circlet of looking-glass' appeare, so that there is a make believe ef utility as well as real pleasure to be afforded by the , The new gem-set lace inuhquestionably very beautiful, bue a possibility only to the really weolthy. At the Opera, throatlets of black Chantilly, set and edged with gems, are well to the fore, and similar bands of less pronounced brilliaccy, are also worn with the new bodices, which boast no collars at all The revival of the old fashion of wearing jawelled lace seems to haVe originated in the idea that this style of decoration was more in accord with the general court mourning. If et surviv 5, it will no! of course, he lone before we shall see all sorts of imitation "jewelled lace" affecte6 try less distinguished folk. It obtained a good place to start wilh.andetwas incepted by an overwhelming majority in the Please of Commons But here its brief and promising nareer ends, since its xt stage is down for Wednesday the 5-h of i June, while the House of Commons stands adjourned mow the holidays, until the next day. The Marriage Law Reform Ass, elation, made an appeal to the Government to shorten the Whitsuntide recess, in order to save the Bill but the request met with no suecesa and once more the Bill fails. tnreugh one of those misehance.,whimi some- bow or other, ever seem to stand In its way. .

THE LADDER OF GUILT.
By ULYSS ROGER%
Author of "For Love and the _Queen," "Weddell
in Mystery," dtn,
CHAPTER XIX.
PROVIDENCE INTERVENES.

"It was nothing very much," continued Martin. "Nine people out of ten would have failed to see salvation in it, for it was merely a disused wicker basket, such as the market people bring fruit to town in. It was water-logged, and lay amidst the mud and sedge near the bank. "Quick as thought I waded into the water and seized the basket. Emptying it of the water, I put it over my shoulders, and, with my head thus hidden from view, waded out further and further into the stream. The cold, icy water seemed to numb every joint of my body, but I went out deeper and deeper, until at length I was borne from my legs and carried along by the current. very slowly I moved. The stream did not rut faster than a mile an hour, and I could merely tread water and allow myself to drift, the basket above completely hiding my head from view. "Suddenly on the bank not twenty yards above me appeared the pursuing warder. I could see him distinctly between the wicker ribs of the basket, though he could not see me. He looked this way and that, and was thoroughly baffled. Once his attention was attracted to the basket floating 1, tranquilly down the stream, and I saw him raise his rifle casually and take aim. The bullet struck the basket and glinted off. Possibly he thought it had penetrated the wicker-work and that I must have been hit had I been inside. But, at any rate, he devoted no more attention to it. "Instead, he walked up and down the stream bank searching for my footsteps. He found them, I am positive, for I saw him follow some track down to the edge of the stream where I had waded in after the basket. Then he looked to the other side, as though searching for me on the far bank. I thought once he was going to plunge into the stream and swim across; but he thought better of it, and hunted further down stream ahead of me, looking, I doubted not, for my footsteps returning shoreward again, after attempting to delude him into the belief that I had swum the river. Then he turned up the bank again and disappeared in the darkness. "I was freezing with the terrible cold, yet I daren't venture out upon the bank until it lias quite dark, for I knew not at what moment he might return, perhaps with reinforcements, to hant me down. But at length it became pitchy dark, and I struck out with my cramped limbs for the bank opposite to that from which I had entered the water.

"There I lay, as though in a dead swoon, scarcely able to move arm or leg, so utterly paralysed was I by the extreme cold. But I bethought that to lie there and die was a worse fate than giving myself up to the warder, and I summoned up all my fortitude and crept on along the bank. Two miles lower the stream was spanned by a railway bridge, and just as I arrived at this spot I heard an approaching train. "My first thought was to slink under the bridge until the train had passed, but a second thought decided me upon using the train to assist me in making good my escape. It was a slow coal- laden train, and just as the last truck crawled over the culvert I darted out from the embankment ' where I had lain in the darkness, with a desperate bound seized upon the buffer, and by a terrific effort dragged myself up on to the top of the truck. There I lay panting, whilst the engine snorted along into the blackness of the night, carrying me mile after mile further and further away from Minewood and the warders and the villarmrs, who by this time were probably all engaged in the man- hunt for me and for Manton. "How far we had travelled I could not say, probably fifteen or twenty miles. But presently the train began to slacken down, and, glancing over the top, I could see the lights of a wayside station. As quickly as I could I slipped from the truck, and as the train slowed down dropped to the line. There were thick trees at this point, and here I harboured while I tried to take my bearings. "I judged it must have been nearly nine o'clock at night. I had tasted nothing since my midday meal, and my limbs were-iced and cramped. To stay out for the night in those wretched clothes was to court almost certain death, whilst as long as I kept my prison uniform on every moment was fraught with the possibility of recapture. "Little by little, therefore, I stole out. There

was a labourer's cottage down the 144 a white- • washed cottage standing back in an acre Of ground. , A ,light shone from a downstairs window. I deter- mined to make for the light and see what luck it would bring me. - "The cottage seemed empty. Evidently the labourer and his wife had gone off into 1 the adjacent village, perhaps to get in their Christmas cheer, or to spend the evening at a friend's house, leaving the light to guide their return. "Cautiously I tried the door. It was locked. . Then I made my way round to the back .i A scullery window was unfastened, and I twisted my body through the small aperture and was inside., There was no sound; nobody was about. "Hungry as I was my first business was to get change of clothes. For that purpose I made my way quietly upstairs. There was a dim night-tight burning in the back room" 'sad the door was open, so that I could peep in. There, .sleeping in a Itiny cot, was a little child. I forgot the clothes, fdrgot any cold and hunger in gating upon the most beautiful sight my eyes had seen for many weary months. Except as we hastily/lased through station after station on our way -to Minewood, I ,had seen no child or woman since I entered opon my term 'of imprisonment for life. ,„• 'For twelve Months I had associated with criminals, lived in an atmosphere crime-laden. The tender sleeping babe awoke a strange feeling in my heart and brought a lump into my throat. If I were caught again and taken back to Minewood, I thought the sight of the exquisite innocence embodied in that cot was worth all the risk, all the trouble, all the danger. I stooped down and kissed the child, and it awoke and commenced to 'cry. Even then I did not think of my danger, but stopped and rocked the infant off to sleep again. • "Then once more I continued my search. I found these clothes in 'a cupboard, 'and tied my own in a bundle and pushed them high up a chimney in a disused room. ' "Downstairs I found food, and I ate ravenously, warming myself at the embers of a fire. 'After- wards I stuffed my pockets full of , bread and cheese, and then quietly closing the door behind, me I made off into the darkness of the night once more. To aid myself I had been guilty of the only crime of my life, but I will repay threefold 'later on. "I wandered out and found an old outhouse on the edge of a wood, and there I remained for the rest of that night and the whole of the next day. I wiis not disturbed. The next night I carefully made my way after dark hack to the neighbourhood of the station, and waited for a goods train travelling. Londonwards. One came at last, and, adopting my previous device,l succeeded in clamber- ing on to the buffer. But, the last coror•artment was the guard's van; and there was no (+lnce of gaining the shelter I had obtained before. How- ever, using all my strength, 1 managed at length to clamber right on to the top, and there I lay face downwards for four hours. I stole off just before we reached the junction at Silent, two miles from ` here, made my way over the Downs, 'and here jam." ,"You will stay with 'us as long as you wish," said the farmer. "Thank you," replied Martin. "I had thought to go up to the Chase and gain the protection of. my cousin for a time. There are rooms in that old house in which I might have hidden for years without even being detected by the servants. I should not be the first fugitive that Lad sought rano nary there." "But you will not go?" queried Cirace,, anxiously. "Not now, after what you have told me to-night. It would be putting too great a temptation in Douglas's way. .I must think out some other course. It will be a couple of months before I dare venture to make my way to the Cape as I intend to do." Farmer Hendon looked' at the clock. "Tt is nearly three," he said. "Hadn't you better get some rest?" - "I am dead beat," replied Martin, "but I dare not sleep. The warders may be even now close upon my track. 'They are bloodhounds in their I- human scent."

But Farmen. !Tendon persisted. "I will keep watch," said he, "if that will satiify your mind. You take my room and I Will stay clown here, though I have no fear of interruptionf, A rest, if only for a few hours, will make a new man of you." They persuaded him at length, and he went %Wain. What a change the warm feather bed

was to his own hard plank at lifinewood ; how luxurious the farmer's plainly-furnished apartment seemed to the bareness and discomfort of the cell wherein he had last slept I He was too much fatigued to think long of these matters. Certain that the watch downstairs would be well maintained he quickly divested himself of his boots, leaped into bed, and in a trice was fast asleep.

div.head: CHAPTER XX.
div.p: CHAPTER XX.

POLICE-CONSTABLE PERKINS'S "STROKE OP LIICK." The old clock in the corner ticked on as the farmer in the easy-chair blinked and smoked. It was a hard task, this self-imposed duty of main- taining watch during the hours which for over sixty years he had devoted to the exigencies of sleep, but he tried hard to keep his senses and succeeded. The clock chimed the half-hour, the three-quarters, and finally struck four., To rouse himself the old man went to the window and looked. out. It was still snowing fast, and the wind was driving the snow in drifts against the window-pane. It was a dark, eerie night. He went back to his seat by the fire, and as he did so fancied he heard a sound outside. "The wind," he muttered to himself, but he bent his ear ...owards the window all the same and listened intently. "Click!" It was the garden gate. "Low must have left it unfastened," he said. "Strange how nervous one gets when one is about at unaccustomed hours and by oneself." "Click!" The gate creaked again. "I suppose I shall get no peace until I go down and shut it," he muttered. "Ugh ! I don't like the idea. It's cold enough even by the fire. However, here goes if I'm not to be worried by it all the rest of the night." He put on his hat and tucked his collar up intending to make a run for it and stop the evil He opened the door and then stood stock still, frozen with terror and amazement, for coming up the path towards his house were four or five men. Their object was self-tvident, for, even though the snow would in itself have been sufficient to smother all sounds of footsteps, yet in their great anxiety they were walking on tiptoe. They saw the door open and made a rush for it. But Farmer Hendon was too quick for them, and ere they reached it the bolts were drawn again. I Then he ran to the foot of the stairs and called: I

"Martin The police 1 The police !" Martin needed no other rousing. He had not removed his clothes, simply his boots, and he was out of bed almost as the alarm was uttered. His wits, sharpened by the terrible experiences he had undergone, told him that, whether he escaped or was captured, it would fare hardly for the old man if he were detected keeping watch. "Come up, Mr. Hendon," he cried. The old man hurried up the stairs, whilst the men outside battered again and again on the door, shouting loudly for admittance. "Quick Undress," said Martin. "They must not know that you have been a party to harbouring me. Let it be thought that I have broken house. Open the window and parley with them as soon as you are undressed. They must believe you have been asleep." "And you?" "There is no hiding-place, no way of escape from the rear ? "

"Yes, yes," said the old man, eagerly. "A skylight from the lumber-room next to this one will let you out on the roof. Thence you can easily step across on to the barn at the back of the house. It is an easy drop again to the ground." "Here goes, then. Good-bye. My grateful thanks if- you don't see me any more." He left the room and was crossing the landing when a vision in white appeared. It was Grace, with frightened eyes and quivering lips. "0 Martin ,What—"

But he had pressed her to his heart. Before she could speak further his lips, were upon hers in loviro, emphasis. "Good-bye, dearest. lam going to make one last bid for it. Bark at their clamouring. They will have the door down in a minute. Remember, whatever happens, you are mine, always, till I am dead."

"Always, Martin," she said, the hot tears cours- ing down her cheeks, "always. God be with you." He tore himself from her embrace and entered the spare room to which the farmer had directed him. Grace, trembling from head to foot, slipped back to her .roorr, her heart uttering a prayer that her lover might escape. The 'clamouring had ceased now, for Farmer Hendon had opened his bedroom window and was holding a parley with the men. If they would wait a moment he would come down and open the door for them. They were free to make what search of his house they might like.

Meanwhile Martin had gained the roof. The snow lay deep, but, by ,dropping into a channel between two slanting portions of the building, he found that he could make his way to where 'he could just see the,white toplof the barn-beneath. It was a drop of 'elight.or tin feet, with a sloping surface to alight upon, but Martin successfully managed it,' and in a twinkling had half-leaPe& half-fallen, from the edge of the stable.to the ground. He Was picking himself up, ready to make a run for it under cover of the . outhouses to the woods beyond, When there was a hoarse chuckle behind hint, and before he was off his hands a huge weight fell upon him bearing him helpless to the ground again. A pair" of hard, rough hands caught at his neck from behind, and the knees of a powerful fellow wormed their way, into the small of his back. He witeignominioully captured without even having the chance of striking a blow in his own behalf. "Thought' yerself clever, eh, sneaking off that way, did yer 11—Help Perkins! Police I—As though I wasn't watching yer little game. Come on all of yer' I've got 'im. This ought ter mean a bit of rhino to me, Ha, ha! And to think Zeke Parr would ever 'a the pleasure of scotchin' yer,; you of gverybody, like this." . His flngetti twined round Martin's throat, and he durhis nails viciously into the prostrate man's neck. "Lor It does my soul good, this does. Lie quiet!" He released one hand and gave • Martin a sledge-hammer blow with it across the bark of the head. "Come on, Perkins Every- body!" His cries had been heard, and at that moment Perkins, the local constable, and the men with him rounded the corner of the stable. "Well caught, Zeke," said the constable. "Don't loose him till I've got the bracelets on. There, that's all right. Now he won't do much damage. Come on, get up. We want yer to come -- With tie. My goodness, to fancy him coming all the way up here and we to have the luck to catch ' him right at home, so to Speak. Quick march. We needn't trouble them in the house any more." They passed under Grace's window. She was there, looking out, and Martin glanced up and saw her. Neither spoke. Her heart was too broken for that, and he had too great a fear that words alight inculpate those who had proved so true to him.

"I can't get over this stroke of luck," said the constable. "Zeke, you're a Briton. I wish that I may never more have to do a similar office for you as I have done, you know, many a time. How the goodness did you get to know of his where- abouts ? " . . .

"Seen him," said Zeke. "Seen 'im go into the 'ouse. I was a-walkin"ome after singing with the waits." The constablb interrupted with i loud peal of lam:alter. • "Waitin' for no good, I'll be bound." "An' jest as I was a parsin' th' farm who should I see but my lord 'ere a-prowlin' about the place. I seen 'im open the latch, an' I didn' wait fur nothin' I can tell 'ee, fur I guessed 'e was arter the young 'ootnan. So I started off fur all I was worth and brought 'ee the news. There'll be a reward for catchin' 'en. Don't forget I'm in that." "I shan't forget," said the constable. "There ain't no need for me to come any further, said Parr, when they reached the fork in the road from which his way home branched, "so _'ll Say good-night. Maybe yer won't take 'im any further than Fenw:ck to-night. I'll look round in the inornin' jest to see how that reward 'll shape. Good-night.' He hurried Alone the road towards the wood. There was a light in the house. Opening the door he stepped in. His mother and Low were sitting (Ater the tire. "Well t " said Low, rising to meet him. "they've got i'im." "Alive 1'" "Alive." "Was that the only way ?" "Perhaps not," said Parr ; and he related the method of Martin's capture. • "You blundering idiot!" cried Low. "It would have been so easy, too; and well worth your while, 1111 told YOU before you started.

"Hold hard, Mr. Low,- saw Zeke. -Don't 11 so 'andy with the names. I ain't gob' to '•11 that on my conscience yr& you've got on yowl, and don't you make no mistake. The next 0,1 from Fenwick wot gets the rope sentence won't? so lucky as the last, nor yet so little deservin' of It An' I don't want to be the next. Try it for your self if yer wants work of that kind done." "Well spoke, Zeke, my son," put in the 0,11 hag, "Not meanin' no offence, Mr. Low," added. "But my boy is everything to me. 'olds yer secret (Low winced) an' we means 'old it as long as you 'bides fair by the under standin'. But if there's any more blood-spillin. to be done, don't yer get my boy to do it. Do ! yerself, for as sure as any 'arm conies to through you, I'll blab. Remember that." The old woman had risen while she was talkill and approached Low, shaking a skinny forefinger s him in emphasis of" her threat. The Parrs wer very forceful argumentators when their blood yr,' up, and Low thought it wise not to continue conversation. "Oh, that's all right," he said. "You needo' trouble about that. No harm will come to Zek through me. I only thought that to-night perlig an accident— a lt would save a lot of bothet and have been better all round, for you especial But, good-night. I shall make it right for yo Zeke, for this night's work. Good-night." He made his way back to the Chase, mutter'' as he went and cursing young Parr for hatiP failed him in the accursed suggestion he had Pu, into his mind. One swift blow with the heavy stir; Parr had would have removed all difficulty al have been considered legal in the man-hunt of Now that Martin had had an interviel
with Grace all Low's troubles and difficulties woe be repeated. Whilst Martin was above ground would be as futile to endeavour to move Grace go influence one of the stone statuettes in the old Cho'
garden. He let himself in quietly and •went to his r But he did not get into bed. His mind was full of dark plans and plots to think of sleep.
CHAPTER XXI.

div.head: WHAT HAPPENED IN THE PUNISHMENT CELL.
div.p: WHAT HAPPENED IN THE PUNISHMENT CELL.

The "cat" was very busy at Minewood duni Christmastide, for of all the convicts who h broken prison not a single one had made go his escape. Manton, it appeared, had remain secluded within thirty miles of Minewood tint driven by hunger and exhaustion, he was forced raid a farmhouse, when he was detected a ignominiously captured. Martin had given the greatest trouble, and gr( was the joy in the Governor's heart at the recei of the telegram announcing his capture. When length the runaway was brought back to the gt the governor ordered his immediate appearsr before him.
The facts of the escape were formally repeated a warder. •

"Have you anything to say for yourself ? " ask the governor. "Nothing," said Martin. "I admit the offence "The full number of strokes with the cat and t irons. And guard yourself very carefully for t future," warned the governor. 'You will find of little use to give trouble here. Take him aws9 He was not punished that day, for the form of medical examination had to be gone through, 51 the doctor was away for a couple of days on leal But at length he was led into the punishment 6 and commanded to strip to his waist. There was another man on the other side of ti cell also engaged in the same operation. Present he looked round, and Martin saw that it °, Manton, the leader of the revolt, the friend 0' had saved him from being recaptured through treachery of Hawkins. Manton's turn came first. He was led up tt), great steel triangle or tripod that stood in t' middle of the room, the centrepiece of a number„ strange inquisitorial objects—manacles, handcum chains—which decorated the cell.

His hands were handcuffed together, and the were slung up to a little chain that hung frota pulley at the top of the tripod. Then his feet' fastened to the bases of the supports, so that I stood with legs outstretched, utterly helpless to off the least resistance. -

Swish! The nine-corded tails came down Wtil all the force of the warder's might across victim's back. Swish I Again, and again, 1111 again the strokes fell, yet no sound escapecl,,,. sufferer. It was not until the sixteenth cut, 11" ti; cut right into the very flesh and drew blood,: Harold Manton suffered a word to escape his I'PB "Stop Stop!" he cried. "I can't bear DO now. I appeal to the doctor:" The doctor was standing opposite looking unconcerned. The warder hesitated and looks the medical man.

"Go on," said the doctor, nonchalantly. The warder seemed to put more power into heavy strokes, and the red flesh marks were sco all over Manton's back. The poor fellow borne up as well as he could, but now with e blow he poured forth piteous groans mingled 0 fierce ,curses against the man who was indict the penalty. But the more he raved against, man the heavier did the blows become. • warder seemed to concentrate all his brutality i the task before him. ,

Manton had received two dozen strokes and 115` yet a dozen more to come unless he fainted rigli away, when the doctor happened to turn his Quick as thought the warder, giving full vent to vindictiveness within him, struck the wretched trs, at the tripod a stinging blow across the head. cords of the cat twined around the poor felloo face and blinded his eyes. He gave vent to aOs of agony. The doctor turned quickly for an explanatio,l3 but before any statement could be volunteered If, warder was struck a heavy blow across the f_TI which felled him. Above him stood the )11", stripped form of Martin, holding the wardet whip, which he had snatched from his fingers. , "You cowardly cur You brute I saw dastardly blow. I--" He said no more, for a truncheon crashed his head, and he fell as though dead to the .11 the cell.
(To be continued.)

But, gentlemen, to sum 111) e,_ e attack under this head they all amount to an s:'elapt to make a defeoce of the Government policy in %tto Africa a sine qua non, of Imperialism. I (lemur to O irt fact, retuse to admit anything of the kind. ii,tore I deal with the question of Imperialism I would 4‘lt to refer to the stupid charge that we are trying to 41tages TEE CHARACTER OF THE BRITISH SOLDIERS. itjhiS IS an abominable and an unfounded insinuation, iust one of those bits of false coin that innst be ari'Led hard to the counter as fast as it is put into maul- Ih,--`• We know perfectly well, as the chief organs of s4:•lberal Press hays pointed out often enough that th or 1„491 soldier has shewn more humanity in the conduct oth"h"la warthan would have been sbewn by perhaps any altt': soldiers in the Zworld. As to farm-burning and kltieverity of that kind we know perfectly well from tl,l who have had to do the work how hateful it was ,tat r,,trtt to have to carry out such policy. They are 40(117te responsible for it than for the diplomacy that t1e51.1) to the war. If the politician led us into difficul- thla:bs soldier is not responsible. (Hear, hear.) Please tob 'lsland that I do not refer to criticisms in Warring- the o ' the ob•a t f which has been to attempt to put us in • c 4ii.'Bltion of detract n.s of either our regular or our thrkt iss7 forcm. lam happy to say that Ido not think thih„°u.s Political opponents here have descondA to any- hetraN the kind, but part of the Tory press in the and unfortunately that part of it which has a 4 ria' circulation has done so • By all means let us have 'treglijt A.frica •by all means let us pay to our forces seiiii:at and auxiliary alike the respect we feel in our tty towards those who in that barren and arid noun- extrtqt merely in the hour of danger in the glamour and fou,:ment oi the early stages of the war which have the Cedi but in the long wearisome months have borne 'tr. 9.‘sden and heat of the day with unflinching tenac- s•-•--..211n_e grt further ' I noticed a suggestion that

the ladiea ah3uld with-hold their favours from everyone wi.o had not held some commission in His Majesty'a forces. I shall not go that far. (Laughter.) Et would be severe on some of us who, eithPr out of deference to a q lak .1' ancestry or the pacific tenden- cies inherited front them, do not feel ourselves so wall out out for that sort of thing. As it is I think the plumes and flohing scarlet have already caught the fancy of the fair sex,—qtaite right too for they are the symbn of bravery and chivalry. (Cheers.) But strange to say our fair friends are apt to overlook the squalid horrors, the untold rnhery, the waste and desolation caused hy warfare. (Heir, hear.) It isiquite right tor our soldiers to be full of fight, it is an awfully diffPrent thing for our statesmen to egg them on to it. Nave take

THIS QUESTION OF IMPERIALISM. What are the real tan is, when we leave the foolish call- ins of names out of iccoult and look the situation in the face. We are all Imperialists, but there are two kinds of Imperialism. One sane. the other foolish and spendthrift. (Hear, hear.) One can show his love for the Empire its other ways than by clam -wring for addi- tion after addition to the Empire. Very few have any idea as to the ex :eat of our Empire. Mirk Twain in his" NI ire Tramps Abroad ' says," The Edglish are mentioned in the Bible "Messed are the meek for they sh ill inherit the eartii." (Laughter Di you know tnat this empire of ours comprises one fourth of the whole hribi!able surface of the globe. Yit if any Liberal ventures to suggest that we do not need to go on annexing vast and often waste tracts he is called a "Litrle Englander" and other ooprobrious names. Now Gentlemen, this E npire carries with it great responsi- bilities. Do you remember the weighty w iris of Lord ssebery some five years ago He pointed out that during the previous twelve years we had Added some 2,600,000 -guars miles of territory to the Empire and added, "that marks out fir maly years a policy from which you cannot depart, if N 011 would, You may be compelled to draw the s rori —I b ye You may not be— but the foreign policy of Gre it Britain until its territory is c )isoli 4 aced, UFO up, settle I, eivilised, must inevitably be a policy of nese" " (Cheers.) Now these are wise words, and they are not the opinion of a " Little E glander " but of an tack owledged Imperialist. Lord it Hebery says that the policy of this country, unless we are forced ha-o war must be a policy of peace. We are at war, and for the present I wish to leave the rights and wrongs of that question aside, and deal with the importance of peace to us as a nation as Lord Rosebery has pointed out. The war is costing we are told a million and a nalf a week, though I am afraid that is an underestimate, But still worse than the money cost is the loss of the brave youna lives, the desolation and misery carried into thousand; of homes. Now I know that some of the staunchest friends of Liberalism in Warrington regard it as just and neces- sary, and sai that sooner or later it wouti have had to come. To my mind that is the only ground on which it can he defendenr—Lord 11)sebery'5 view—that it is a clash of civilisation, and it was better to get it over, On the other hand there ars many who have all along denounced the war as unnecessary and criminal. Let us at once admit these differences of opinion amongst our friends, it is better to do So. But thsre has been no division of opinion on the question of voting supplies ; we have stinted neither men nor money. THE CONDUCT OF THE .LIBERAL PARTY has been, I think, admirable in that respect, and the accusation levelled at us for party purp ,ses of being unpatriotic is sheer nonsense. (Cheers.) We condemned both the policy that led up to the war, at d the manner in which the Gaverament has condtwted that war. The lack of preparation, the continual undet-e•tl metre of our toe's strength ; the nee Bess severity of the policy of farm burning and desolation ; end abovs all the mistake of not building that bridge over which the enemy could have climbed down, leaving us with all we actually required in the way of peace con- ditions, and yet without making them feel absolutely crushed, embitterei an i disgraced. (Cheers.) Leaving humanity out of account, it is the greatest tactical error to drive brave men to desperation ; to make them feel that pe ice can only be ob'ained on what they con- sider disgraceful terms. The Government really seems to think that human nature is different in South Africa to what it is here. (Hear, hear.) lam not going to trespass on your time and patience by going over the old ground of tbe diplomatic despatches. The more I think of the history of the negotiations the more lam convinced that wih patience and Wise statemanship the war could have been and ought to have been avoided. (Cheers). Yoa know the great reason for the war was the relief of the Uitlanders. People are inclined to talk as if the liitiander opinion was all one way; they forget the thousands who fought against US. I am going to quote

THE OPINIONS OF AN lIITLANDER who is not one of them • On the contrary he is a merchant in London, who recognises as much as any of us that now we have got to fighting the Union Jack must fly in the end over thee countries and that it would be not only against oar interests but against the interests of civilisation and of trade if there were any other result. I think our Tory friends should pay some attention to this Uitlander because he is no altruistic visionary or political wind bag, but the head of a powerful firm of merchants in Lmdon who do—or did—a very large trade in the Trans- vaal and the Orange Free Sc;ate, an I who in short have a very large stake in the country. I may say he has been at times a purchaser of same very excellent manu- factures turned out at Bank Q lay. (Laughter.) I know they tell you the Boers do no: wa,h, but don't believe that. (Laughter) And it was in this connection I called upon him in 1898 This was about the time of the pathetic appeal from certain gentlemen on the Rand on behalf of the women and children and other op. pressed Uitlanders and I asked this unfortunate mer- chant, who was one of them what we Ought to do to help them. He said," For Heaven's sake leave us alone," and he told rce what 1 dare say you saw Mr Morley mentioried at Carnarvon when he warned us against rushing into this war,—that the British working man out there in the mines was earning his pound a day and seeding home ample supplies to his wife and family in Cornwall, better, I fear, than be will ever be able to send again. And as for the poor down-trodden capitalist —(taughter),—well, my informant is not interested in the mines, but the whole bulk of his trade was that of a Conerst merchant and distributor chiefly in the Orange Free State and the Transvaal. Be is not interested in concessions from the Transvaal Government. The firm with whom my friend is connected are merchants doing business in the ordinary way, and he told me their profits for the previous year were well into six figures sterling. (" Oh.") It so happens that a few months afterwardst Mr Chamberlain invited the gentleman to whom I allude to give him his views at the Colonial Office. Yes, and what did he tell Mr Chamberlain and his subardinates?—"That the Transvaal and the Orange Free States were two ripe plums that would fall into John Bull's mouth ; That nothing excepting England's mistakes could prevent within a generation, federation coming about in South Afaica in the crdinary course of trade and with the influence of wealth and population." I have not seen my friend slime 1E96 till the beginning of this year, when I called on him again in London. I should like you to have heard him. Be regards this war from our point of view, as a colossal blunder. (Loud cheers.) What is it from a South African point 'of view? Nothing less than—in the words John Bright used long ago about another war•-•" A measureless calamity." (Cheers.) He assures me it has been engin- eered as certainly by the dominant capitalists there— who thought it good business—as that same shady gang , engineered the Jameson raid. (Shame.) Chamborlain • at a distance has been misled, and the influences and deception brought to bear, or the temptation of ambi- ; tion, or both has been too much for him. It is

tEhLeL oTyOlt iTt LoYf OoFu r TcHoEl nRiEeDs EtTeNcipluFEckATUaßnEdS oti fUttlVe Erarsv, patriotism, the tenacity and gallantry of our soldier 4, these are redeeming features and the revelations that have come to light may be an excellent lever for carry- ing reforms, but does anyone suggest that this is the slightest excuse for rushing into the war. It is had enough for us to lose so many thousands of 1111 flower of our manhood, but what is it for the people on the spot? What is the best safeguard in Continental Europe to-day against a conflagra 19n. Simply the experienee they have had Of war at their own doors. If we knew something of that in this country—which Heaven forbid should ever be the case—the Jingoes would be less ready to" Let slip the dogs of war," We do not find that the soldiers, the men on the spot are the ones who denounce our foes. No, it is the man who takes care of himself at home. There was a little paper, a humour- ous and charming prldaction, written and illustrated by our soldiers in Pretoria in the compound. It was called the" Waterfall Wag" and I dare say some of you have seen the facsimile sicce printed. I have a Copy in my hand, this is what they say of the Boers :—" In conciusion we may sty the Boers have proved them- selves a valiant foe and as such have earned the respect of their conquerors. This ui he case we look for- ward with confidence to the not far distant future when Boer and Briton will join hands in friendship—a friend- ship that will become fast when they know us better and find that revenge is no part of our nature and that they are allowed to enjoy the tights and privileges which were denied to us." There is an honest ring about this one is thankful to bear much in contrast to the vile Yellow Journals of London. The press may think such attempts to play to the gallery are patriotic but I con- sider them vulgar and disgracefuLand quite 'in-English. WHAT OF THE FUTURE This war has put out of sight reforms which year by year do not grow less urgent. First there is the cause of temperance and the far reaching effects—beneficial— of Lord Peel's Minority Report which will, I have no doubt be appreciated by many of my bearers better than I can appreciate it but I think it will appeal to all im- partial people and I think it will carry a great weight of public opinion with it. I am sure that support to that measure will by no means be limited to party lines and I believe that many an honest person will lhave a twinge in opposing what is so obviously for the good of the country. Then we have to consider the very im- portant question of taxation and here I really do not see that you can hope for any great reduction in the enormous annual expenditure we have now reached. surely that only makes it the more necessary to com- plete our reforms in the incident of taxation. div.head: 1H14.: EXAMINKR, FRIDAY, MAY 31 1901
div.p: 1H14.: EXAMINKR, FRIDAY, MAY 31 1901

' the taxation of ground rents and the un-earned meat, questior s with which we shill be forced to del. As regards the reformi which Lord Stanley and the Duke of Devonshire may be to) public spirited to con- demn in their hearts, the point is that we Liberals have to supply the motive power. These are no academic subtleties, for we can trace the close connec- ace and the far reaching infiumce on the daily life of the people which these reforms will have. They in ay therefore fire every good patriot with just the same enthusiasm which carried the great reforms of old days. Let us oat forget those great predecessors, ad the noble example which Walpele and Chatham, Burke and Fox, Peel and Cobden, Bright and Gladstone have left us in measure. which t 3 quote one of our old members, expressions " have made the fame of states- men and the glory of the nation." The life work of these men has helped to mould the character of our people and I say! that is a great heritage for us all What m-tter if we are in the cold shade of opposition. Remember Victor Hugo'

fine aphorism, ....Bucc,.ss is a dangerous word, its resemblanc Ito merit deceives mankind." Lot us rather be glad it is not all fine sailing right away, and that we have a chance to wire our spurs. N)w, gentlemen, is it altogether worthy of our town to reap all these good things and never help at the sowing? I appeal to all who are not the mere slaves of use and wont, and who have at heart equally the good of their town and their country. These reforms are measures of expediency and of justice, and I think we have a right to ask our friends in Warrington to help these great causes onward. If I may quote one of the noblest and most lofty minded men now living, who in spite of all the vulgar sensa- tionalism of the day, the hocus pocus of party dodges and attempts Co excite and befool the gallery, still com- mands by his integrity, unswerving courage and fidelity to principle, and to that ideal which even in these shallow days still remains the obj-,ct of such a man's life, and to ask our friends to help to " swell the force- of that tide of opinion on the force and set of whose [current depends the prosperous voyaging of humanity." (Appliiuse). • COUNCILLOR PIERTIINT AND ME WAR, 001100illOr PIERPOINT, in seconding the resolution, Said he Claimed to be a Liberal; but he was a Litteral ot the old type, and he wished there were more ot them in Warrington. He was ashamed of the Liberal party as at present constituted, and he was not altogether pleased with their chairman, but he gave him the fullest and completest absolution. (Laughter). At the time of the last election the whole country, with very few (iv:options, had gone stark, staring, mad about patriotism. (Hear, hear.) They called it patriotism : in his opinion it was all gerrymandering on the part of the Unionist party of the country. He did not blame the Tory party—it was natural to them to do these things—but he blamed the powertul interest of the Unionist party. Toe Liberal party contamed, in his opinion, a number of men who were sailing under the guise of the name of Liberal, and who were as Unionist as Joseph Chamberlain. (Hear, heat.) Joseph Cham- berlain and the gang to which Mr. Crosfield had referred were responsible for the war, and if there was a Provi dence who metei out punishment to men for committ- ing a great wrorg to an individuaLhe hoped that punish- ment would be accorded to men who had done a great wrong to us as a nation. They talked about corruption in the Transvaal, let them wait ten years and then they would see what the Liberals would say, and what the Tories would admit—that the war in the Transvaal was BEGOTTEN IN INFAMY, AND CARRIED OUT WITH CRUELTY and was a disgrace to us as a nation. Re had not come prepared to say a single word, exeept on what had arisen through the speech of Mr. Croafield, and perhaps he was saying rather more than he ought to say, but it was in him—he could not help it. He could see the Boers being treated in a manner to which he objected, becauie he considered that the inception of the war was absolutely, wrong and ought never to have been brought about. Therefore if he held these views, he wait per-

fectly justified in feeling indignant at the progreis of the war. Be did not blame the soldiers, it was part of their trade. This was an opportunity they had been waiting for ever since the last great war we had. The first great war they recollected was the Crimean war. Everyone knew the object of that war. The money we spent and the lives that we lost were thrown away in a wrong cause,and what we tried to effect then,had been absolutely nullified, and they admitted that the Crimean war was a mistake. But they did not say that the soldiers engaged in the war did wrong. They served their country as well then as the army had served their country in the Tgansvaal. The latter war was at first supposed to be a military parade—merels- sailing to Gagetown and coming back again. We sent the raw , material of the army in the shape of privates up to non- commissioned officers. As far as the fighting power was concerned he believed that was as good an army as we could send out. Ele was not going to hold the soldiers responsible for THB MANY DIA:INDERE MADE _

- by the men placed over them. It had been a privates' war, and the honour belonged to them, And not to a great number of men who would get all the honour and all the great pensions that would be accorded to them. (Applause.) Mr Crosfield had alluded to cor- ruption. Everybody said the Boers were not to be' trusted for a moment. He denied it. TEE BOERS WERE A HOME LOVING PEOPLE and further than that they were essentially a religious people. The only literature a Boer looked for, and the only literature a Boer wanted wee his Bible and if they were going to try and convince hind that a man who studied his Bible was a blackguard. he was not going to believe them. Yet they said these men were full of corruption—granted. They were like a lot of old , fossilized Tories. THEY WANTED TO GOVERN IN THEIR OWN WAY and they were stupid and insisted on governing in- their own way. They might have a little corruption, but could they tell him of a single Town Council in this country that had not corruption in it ? (Laughter.) This was making it rather strong, but they knew for a positive fact that in every Town Council in the country they had men who were there for their own interests and not for the good of the town ; or else he was'under a wrong impression. He hoped he was, but he had lived a good number of years and he was afraid there was a great deal of truth in it. If the Boers had a little cor- ruption—and we had a little corruption in all our little coteries—what was the corruption of the Boers in com- parison with the financial gang and those statesmen who were interested in gold mines ? The corruption of these gentlemen would be as St. Paul's Cathedral to a little mole hill in a twenty acre meadow. One was very plainly to be seen, and the other, they need not take very much notice of. Be hoped THE LIBERAL PARTY IN WARRINGTON . _ -

would see if they could not go through the fire of purifi- cation. Lt them drop all those Jingo Unionist kind of Liberals—they were no good to them as a party. If they were going to raise a party, he did not care what they called it. If the se-called Jingo Unionist Liblral was determined to retain the name, and if they could not find a better name, lot them adopt the name of socialist. He was not afraid of the name socialist. They must get some name that was striking —call themselves the pure party. But for goodness sake get a party whose principles were based on those great examples, Bright and Gladstone. (Applause.) Let them go through the fire of purification, become honest to themselvm and honest to the people, and not think so much about their gold mines. (Applause).

SOME REMARKS BY CJIIMCILLOR TINNION. The CHAIRMAN said they did not always agree with everything that Councillor Pierpoint said, it was rather a big order. (Laughter.) H I must, say, however,that Councillor Pierpoint bad given egpression to a good many truths, which, after all, in their calm moments, struck home to them with very great force. He (Off chairman) was nut going to discuss the question of the purification of the Liberal party, because he still maia- tained that that part of the Liberal party which was left, did not need very much purification. (Councillor PIERPOINT : I am glad to hear it). He thought the dross had been skimmed off, and what was left had come out of the fire pure and refint.d metal. It was not altogether a question of purification as far as Warrington was coixerned, but of re-organization. What they wanted was to get their organisation as com- plete as that of the Conservative party. If the Liberals of Warrington rallied round a pure standard he did not hesitate to Say that they could win the next election easily, but they could not win it with the present orga- nisation. It was TOO OLD AND FOSSILISED for present day use, it was too rusty. They wanted every member of the Association to know in what position he stood, and what he was prepared to do. If they would reorganise, and utilize all the force they had at their disposal in Warriny,ton, be had not the slightest hesitation in saying that they could win this borough. (Applause.) The resolution was unanimonsly adopted. COUNCILLOR PLUMPTON AND THE WAR. Councillor JAMES Evesis proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman for presiding and to Mr A H Crosfield and Councillor Pierpoint for their addresses. In seconding the motion, Councillor PLIMPTON said that since Mr Crosfield hod come before them he had exercised a spirit of determination that he (the speaker) scarcely expected from him. He was more convinced than ever that he was their candidate of the future and that he would ultimately be the member tor

Warrington. He (the speaker) would never rest satisfied until he saw that accomplished. After referring to the necessity for reorganiz Alen he proceeded to speak about the war in South Africa. He said he had been studying the South African question for a number of years, and he felt coed lent thst we had a battle to fight some day. It had perhaps not been ' brought about in the best way on this occasion, but be felt that the Transvaal Government was not carried on in the proper way. He believed that the Transvaal Government could see that the Uitlanders were getting too numerous and too powerful for the c.tryiLg on of their Government. They tried to rob the Uitlanders of every freedom thst they had. They were determined that the English should have no power there, and that the B)ers should ride triumphant over South Africa. There never was a bigger lot of Tories in this world. (Laugh- ter.) There never was a greater Tory than Kruger— (renewed laughter)—he was the greatest Tory who ever lived—a regular despot. He was not going to give them credit for the way in which the war had been conducted—he thought there had been a great waste of money and power—but he did not think that at the present time if they had a change of government they should improve matters at all. Be should like to see the present govern- ment in office a little longer. it the same time he claimed to be as good a Libsral as Mr Pierpoint or any gentleman in that room, and he should stick to the Liberal cause as long as he lived. (Applause). The motion was carried.

In respending. Councillor PIERPOINT said that every statement Councillor Plumpton had made in disparage- ment of the Boer Government could be controverted and was cOntrovened by the Blue Booki issued by the Tory Government. .

flay! Mesthur Yead-hitter ! Wen thowts cums inter eaur owd gray yeds, heaw good owd Warrin- tun locks neaw cumpared wi twanty yers back, wen aw mysen cams back to 'th owd teawn wonst an away,aw wanthers abeaut 'th differunt sthreets, quite loas-in mysen sum-toimes, an havin to ax tolks which is mi nearest way to 'th "Flashy Bend" as Teawn's End uset bi cawd—whoy, wan aw sit an think aheaut it an, aw connot help but eonsither that raally an truely,aw man be gerrin owd! Wen aw say owd, aw dunno mean feelin tbad way up i th top attick. Nowgh ! By gum! mi braains keeps aw rest, thank Gudnus! Aw knaw them's aw rest, cos t' other day a chap awrn pertly akwaintet wi coom up to mi an ast mi fur 't land him hate a suv- rin ! Aw soon up an towd him that aw beleoved naythur i borrerin nut lendin nil it wad look mooch betther on him if he'd attend his wark a bit oftener, istid o' warein so manny starcht cuffs and collers,an marchin up an deawn 'th streets, so as fur'l, make aw'th yang wimmen think he wur somebry. Nowgh ! ‘th brane pert's pratty soul, but wen aw look at 'th thatch aw reaund it,an heaw that thatch has a varry winthry look abeaut it. Wen aw draws mi bit o'lookin glass a bit nar to mi and sees wot folks caws crows toes making raguler deep loines areaund an below mi boath hies—loines as deep as a Boheer digs his threnchers—then Mesthur Yead- hitter, aw hey to cum to'th conclooshun thad awm gerrin a owd crater. It's a funny thing wi dunnot foind this eawt ourselvs, es a Toole its other foke wot foinds it eaut for us. "Hello! Jack" aw cawd eaut to a trend won day ith streeat " wheer ar tha ' beaunt fur ? " " Wheer theau'rt non whantet " be soon towd mi "thi yures too whoit !" Thad thowt- less :speeuch o his seat mi agate a thinkin. In fakt, it hert mi a bit at'th lost, bur aw sane geet to think thad Jack's crazy tawk afther aw wur a benefut an did mi gad. He war quiot reet—aw shud no bi wantet amung a ruck planty yungar then mysen. Moind yoa, aw dunnot say as'th henergie i. no theer,anplanty on it—this mooch is a fakt,thad awd tawk anny hate duzzen on um—yang uns as weal, , reel unther table wi eaut much adoo. Bud o' cooree thad's nor id. Sum tomes wen one's just ith mid- dui of a noice sooart ny a job summat seems to goo , rung abeaut it an yoa connut finish it ith way ut yoa'd bike. Then yoa thinkun " dang thi, awl chuck thi up, theau botherin foo, and it seems quoite fort eaus (ease) yore moind afther yoa'n laft it uniinisht. Bur it did no use't to be bike thad, a duzzen yet agoo Nowgh! i them days, awd goo at it, hommer and tungs, an afore bein dun bi it, awd bring th job deawn on is hands an knees. But tawkin a bit sin abeaut gad owd Warrintun an th' differunce theer is neaw an twanty yer sin. Hay! Dear ! Th' grass wot use't fur't graw at th' top o' Church-streeth, an a gad lung sthreet it use't to be an is neaw aw reckon. Then sthrait on past 'th woire warks an' th' owd baths. abeaut which aw shun hey a tale fur't tell you abeaut sum day. A bit fart on, yoa cum amung planty o' littul cobbul stooans to to' owd " Ring 0' Bells " wheer Mesthur Taylor,use't bi th'lanlurd. Then aw con remember an owd littul chap caw'd "Billy-Billy." Oh! Dear! moi memrys gerrin fit fur nowt sum toimes• Anny way owd Billy's corner ith' owd tap-room wur alias saved fur him, becos he nary missed a singul fleet i'th' wick cawin in fur his peint or two. An one neat, it wur afore moi toime aw think, but aw've heerd th',tale towd, sum larky raskil reitched deawn owd " Billy" clay poipe frum th' rack wheat he allus left it th' neet'afore. Well this joakin chap an one ur too moore,as monkeyish as he wur crommed a toothri grains o' gun peawder ith poipe yed, an cuyert it oer in a horry with lb leovin's oth bacco owd Bibby had left in oer nest, Then they seat it up back 'wen ith rack wheat it allus hung. Abeaut noiue o'clock ur so thad need in cum 'th owd chap. " Hello ! Willyum ! heavy ar yo t' neat" axt one o'th conspyraturs, whoile aw 'th tothers seet theer, itchin furt 'th owd fella 't teitch up an ger owd uv his poipe. Bur thad ueet,he seeumt rayther moor thowtful than he generally wur, and in no hurri fur hie poipe. T'others begun a fiAgittin fur, they thowt th spooart wur non cumin hoff. "Ar no yoa gooin t hae yore smook to neet. Willy um," at larst axt one o 'th chaps. " High !, Aw t hink aw'l have a th'raw," said th owd felly, an' he reicht up for his favorite clay. Aw tot hers Beet Cheer watchin' every moovmunt. They seed im atom his lift hond little finger inter th' poipa yed th' same as he aullus use't do. Then foindin th' bowl was pretty f all, he reitcht a spill an' bigun leetin it. Yoa met a heard a pin dthrop amung th' rest o' th' chaps. Th' owd felly pood sway, leeted another spill, wot went eaut afore its toims, then he thried a match an' th' poipe seeumt fart' thraw a littul bettlitir. Aw th' chaps had thur heyes starin straight at owd Billy's poipe yed, an they cud see th' red glow on th' top o' th' bacco, whoile th' owd chap's boath cheeks wur sucked in aitch soide uv his face summat bike th' Mins (backs) uv a thin book, coe he'd bin pullin' 90 'lard. Well, it coom at larst ! Aw shud say it went. Fur, dun yoa knaw,th' poipe yed floo up to th' top o' th' seelin' ; thur wur a realur hexploshum just loike, a pistul gooin' off ! Owd Billy jumpt up off his seeut, cum eaut wi' sum pratty strung wards, th' follies i' th' room cudn't aboide for brastin' eaut thiur crazi- nusg, an' they aw rusht to th' doore, bostin thursels wi' larfin, fur they cud keep that faces straight no lunger. Owd Billy run afther um, an' hommert at um lost one, then de tother, till he ad his fisses an nukkels quoite soar! Fur menny a wick afther he use't fancy he'd wur gooin' t hey th roomatiks till aw th swellin' wheat deawn. Fur a lung time, non o' them chaps dost goo near owd Billy uv a neat, for Mu) his fisses wur wake, his tang wur varry raspish, an cud ster sum on urn up aboov a bit. Poor owd chap! hee's gon to his long whoam menny yers sin, an a gad noomber uv his niateys as well. Well ! aw rakin. 'th best way is fur 't bi raddy, an liv accordin' so thad wen eaur poipe yed's abeaut fit fur't thdrop, th hexploshun winno kaus us anny surproise.

div.head: MR. JOHN PEMBERTON'S CASE AGAINST THE CORPORATION.
div.p: MR. JOHN PEMBERTON'S CASE AGAINST THE CORPORATION.

The following is the verbatim judgment (briefly announced by us last week) given in the appeal by Mr John Pemberton for the discovery of documents in his case for a mandamus to inspect the minutes of the Gas Committee of the Warrington Corpora- tion. Loma Jusricn COLLINS—M! Newbolt has said all that could be said I think on behalf of his client in this case but I can see no reason for interfering with the order of the Learned Registrar in Man- chester. The action appears to me to raise nothing but a question of Law that is to say whether the right to inspect given by Section 233 of the Muni- cipal Corporation Act 1882 which says' The minutes of proceeding of the Council shall be open to the inspection of a burgess on payment of a fee of Is and a burgess may make a copy thereof or take an extract therefrom" entitles the burgess to inspec- tion of any Thing other than the Minutes of proceed- ings of the Council. The burgess says it does the Council says it does not. That is a pure question of law, and I can see no issue of fact as to which any document could be said to be relevant. There is no issue of fact and therefore there can be no ' question as to discovery or inspection uf documents. On those short points it seems to me that the learned Registrar was perfectly right and that this appeal must fail. LORD JUSTICE STIRLING: I am 01 the Same opinion. The only issues of fact raised are contained in paragraphs 6, 7 and 8 of the statement of claim and not one of those is traversed or denied by the state- ment of defence. They allege in substance that the plaintiff on certain occasions there specified requested the defendants to produce for his inspec- tion the acts of the Gas Committee submitted far approval to the Council of the defendant Corpora- tion. The defence does not deny the existence of those acts and what is more partly admits them because it states that the defendants deny that the plaintiff at the date mentioned was entitled to have open to his inspection the acts of the Committee submitted for approval to the Council for the year 1900 as recorded in the minutes of the said Committee. That is an admission of the existence of the minutes. Therefore it seems to me that everything which the plaintiff would be called upon to prove at the trial is really admitted and that there is no issue of fact which requires to be decided by a jury The only question is one of law. It seems to me therefore that discovery and inspec- tion are needless. Mr SUTTON : Ido not know whether your Lord- , ship will say anything as to the costs. Lard JUSTICR COLLINS The appeal will be dis- missed with costs. I believe that is generally understood in the Court of Appeal. Ido not think it is necessary to say anything unless something to the contrary is said. I think that is the fact. Is not that so, Mr Pollock? Mr EnNusr Porzocx : I have always understood so, my Lord. The case will now he taken, we understand, be- fore the divisional court, which will decide whether the case is on all fours with the test ca',e of Williams v the Corporation of Manchester, in which the decision was that "the Burgesses were entitled to inspect in future the minutes of all acts of corn. mittees submitted to the Council, whether those acts were finally approved or not."

Sudden Death of Mr Robert Fleming. %Me regret to announce the death of Mr Robert Fleming, which took place at his residence, Kimberley-street,off Upper Parliament-street,liiver- pool, on Saturday morning. Mr Fleming went home apparently quite well on the Friday night.but was taken suddenly ill early the following morn- ing, and although a local medical man was called in, death took place as stated. The deceased, who was 33 years of age, had lived in Liverpool for the last three years, and was a co-manoging director of the firm of J R Fleming and Company, tanners, Fennel-street, Warrington, He leaves a wife and two little children: The cause of death was heart disease. The funeral took place at the Warrington Cemetery on Tuesday afternoon.
