THE COMING TRIALS OF MOTOR VEHICLES.

The third series of trials of m-itor vehicles for heavy traffic is arranged to take place in Liverp)ol and neigh- bourhoOd during the five days commencing Monday, June 3. These trials, like their predecessors, are being organized by the Liverpool Self-Propelled Traffic As.ocia- tion, which, since it initiated these competitions in 1898, has affiliated itself as a' local centre" to the Automo- bile Club af Great Britain and Ireland. In 1898 the ' adaptation of automobilism to heavy traffic was in its infancy, and only four vehicles actually took part in the Liverpool trials of that year. Wittrut exception the wheels of these vehicles proved structurally defective ' when subjected to the hammering action of granite sets and cobble atones, whilst minor troubles arose in respect to adhesion and with the condensers, The second trials, which took plaol in 1899, provided satisfactory evidence that the tire and adhesion difficulties had been overcome, for none of the wheels gave the smallest trouble, and five out of the six c,ompeting vehicles in the hill-zlicabing tests successfully surmounted gradients varying between one in nine and one in thirteen with as heavy a load as six and a half tons. Yet the judges found that the strength of these vehicles was " below , what is compatible with a satisfac •nry life in commer- cial work "—a state of things which they attributed mainly to" the difficulties imposed by meeting the limit of three tons tare under the locomotives on Highways Act, 1898 " In order to see whether manufacturers could improve their designs so as to produce an effi tient commercial vehicle under the three-ton limit of tare, the Liverpool Association have allowed an interval of two years between the second trials and the third series now about to be held. _ _ _

For the coming trials an entry of 13 vehicles has been secured, which will Compete in four classes. Class A is. ior comparatively light 'vehicles propelled by internal combustion engines using deodorized naphtha or petro- leum spirit, and carrying a load ot only one and a half ton. The vehicles entered under the other three classes are all steam propelled, electricity being again unrepre- sented. The steam wagons, however, comprise a great variety of design, including several boilers of the flash, or instantaneous generation, type. For Class A the maximum tare is two tons, and for Class B three tons; but Classes C and D have no tare limit, and these vehi- cles are to be watched specially on behalf of the Local Government Board, with a view to a possible amend- ment of the thri•-on tare limit in the Act of 1896. The trials will be attended by representatives of four Government departments, the High Commissioner for Canada, and five of the Agents-General for the Colonies. The Secretary of State for War has appointed the follow- ing six officers :—Colonel C H Scott, C.8.,R.A-, Lieuten- ant. Colonel F B Elmslie, E,A., Lieutenant-Colonel H CL Holden, R.A., (Superintendent of the Royal Gun Factory), Captain F Lindsay Lloyd, R.E., Captain C Hl3 Nugent,R,E.,and Lieutemint-Colonel R E Crompton,R E The India Office have appointed Coionel Scott, as above wbo is Ordnance Consulting Officer for India, and Cora- ' mender G T Wingfield, R.N., Superintendent of the India Store Department. The Postmaster-General has appointed Mr F Salisbury, postmaster of Liverpool, and the President of the Local Government Board, Mr G W Willcocks,M.l.C.E. Lord Strathcona will be represented by Mr G H Mitchell, of Liverpool. A number of muni- cipal corporations have also intimated their intention of sending deputations to watch the competition, whilst the pleasure side of automobilism will be represented by the leading members of the Automobile Club, who have arranged to tour down to Liverpool direct from the Gordon-Bennett race in Franse.

div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.

Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. There was an average attendance at the meetine of this Society on Sunday. Mr William Beswick presided and in the course of a brief address reminded his hearers of the annual commemoration of the Day of Pentecost and drew from it a useful lesson. Mr Heatan, of Manchester, delivered an earnest address based on the words "He shall baptise you with the Holy Ghost and with fire." The soloist for the afternoon was Mr Arthur Griffiths who gave an effective rendering of " If with all your hearts." Mr Payton, Mu s Sac presided at the organ. The service was also taken part in by the Rev John Yonge (presdent), Messrs Healey and A Downes. Moore Wesleyan Chapel. The anniversary sermons on b3half of the school funds were preached in the Moore Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday, when very I %ego congregations attended. On each occasion Mr J R Posnett, of Runcorn, was the preacher. Special hymns and the anthems " 0 worship the Lord in the beauty of Holiness," and " He shall reign for ever," were well rendered by the choir and scholars. The congregation at the evening service was especially large, the recent addition to the chapel,in the shape of enlarged Sunday school being found very use- ful. The collections at the Close of each service were in support of the Sunday school funds, and realized £l6 93. Daresbury Paris Church. Large congregations attended the services at the Parish Church on Sunday, when the Rev H. Lester, of the Warrington Training College, was assisted by the Rev J Best, Principal of the Cheater Training College, Mr. Best occupying the pulpit at the morning serviceeand Mr Lester at the evening service. At 8 a.m there was a choral celebration of the Holy Communion, at whieh an unusually large number of parishioners oommunicated, Iderbeck's service being well rendered by the choir. div.head: GREAT SANKEY PARISH COUNCIL.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY PARISH COUNCIL.

Sankey Brook Again. • A meeting of the Great Sankey Parish Council was held in the Board Schools, Great Sankey, on TneAay evening. Mr G Thompson presided and there were also present: Messrs T Halton, .7 FUlton Smith, J Kilshaw, W Taylor, with J Smith (clerk).

_ , THE POLICE SERGEANTS RESIDENCE. The Clerk stated that he had written to the Police Superintendent of the Leigb Division informing him that the Council hai appointed a depu'ation to wait upon him with reference to the police arrange- ments of the Sankey district generally, and parti- cularly the question of the newly appointed ser- geant being stationed in Sankey as was formerly the case, He had received a reply to the effect that Superintendent Higginbottom was ill, and on writirig again later was informed that he had left home bar a month. The Clerk was instructed to communicate with the Superintendent when he returned.
EXTRA POSTAL FACILITIES.

Mr HALTON said as one of the deputations appointed by the Council be saw Mr Viney, the Warrington post- master, and represented to him that the Council desired certain increased postal facilities. Mr Vtney met him very courteously and promised to make any concessions which were practicable. Mr Viaey had agreed to the suggestion that any letters received after the usual de- liveries on week days shout] be sent to the Great Sankey Post Ofil:e where they could be called for. The hour ot collection had been extended until 9.20 p.m. on week days and 8.20 on Sundays. The question of establish- ing a telegraph office at Great Sankey would be taken into clasideration.

The Ch airman said they were indebted to Mr HAlton for the trouble he had taken in this matter and to Mr Viney for the generous way in hicti he had treated them, lie moved a vote of thanks to Mr Viney. Mr Halton seconded, M, Fulton Smith supported.and it was agreed to.

THE -ACCOMMODATION AT THE RAILWAY STATION. Mr Fulton Smith drew attention to the subject and said the question of the accommodation at the railway station was one which appealed to most people who travelled by the Cheshire Lines. At present thoae who travelled to Warrington and beyond had to book on one side of the station, and then either cross the rails or go up the steps and round by the road. He moved the following resolution :—" That a representation by this Parish Ceuncil be made to the Cheshire Lines Committee requesting some immediato modification of the present booking office arrangements at Sankey Station, whereby the great inconvenience as well as danger to passengers crossing the rails may be avoided.' _ .
The Chairman seconded, Mr Halton supported, and it was agreed to.
THE POLLUTION OF SANKEY BROOK. STRONG COMPLAINTS.

The Clerk read four letters, complaining strongly of the pollution of Sankey Brook. Mr W D Houghton of Sankey Wire Mills, wrote call- lag attention to the offensive smell from the brook due ing the dry weather. Numerous complaints were being made and he hoped some imm,diate steps would be taken by the sanitary authorities to remedy the evil and relieve the district from this annoyance and danger. Mr W Sloane, of the Mersey White Lead Company, Limited, Sa.lkey Bridges, called attention to foul smells

from the brook. WWI the wind in the direction of his office, the smell was scarely endurable, and ho was apprehensive of mischief arising from the same. He had no doubt the Sankey Parish Council would exercise themselves to protect them against the importation of foreign matter into a district not over effLient in sanitation.

Mr A. E Tonge, oi Sankey Bridges, complained that the question of the pollution of Sankey Brook received no further attention than discussion in the Council Chamber of the Warrington Corporation. The coming hot weather would mean a recurrence of the vile filth this stream gives off, its condition being almost unbear- able and positively sickening, and dreaded by all who were bound to live near it. Property owners were feel- ing its effects in the fact of its tendency to depreciate the value of their property, driving the better class people further away from the bad smells and giving place to a rougher element. The question would have to be dealt with boldly as the present:state of affairs,could not possibly be tolerated much longer. Colonel Ridgway, of Grappenhall Lodge, wrote that if It was in the power of the Council to bring before the proper authorities the abominable stench from the Sankey Brook during the spell of hot and dry weather he hoped they would do what they could as he felt pretty sure that if something was not done they would have diphtheria at Sankey Bridges. The nuisance was caused, as all were pretty well aware by the drainage from the waste heaps add the sewage of St. Helens. He was not aware that any of the Warrington sewers entered the brook at all so he supposed the County Council were responsible for allowing such to continue from St.Helens and if the Council would take the matter up perhape something might be done. The coming summer was not unlikely to be a hot and dry one and with no fresh water going into the brook the result was purely sewage matter and a stench that might be cut with a knife. The Chairman said he came back into the district on Monday from a abort holiday and the stench was really dreadful. He had never smelt the brook so badly before, and he thought if the Council could do anything in the matter they should take some steps. The District Coun- cil, he thought, had taken the matter up. Mr Halton said he had time after time brought the matter to the notice of the District Council. They seemed to think the Warrington Corporation bad more authority to deal with it. He personally thought the two authorities should unite in endeavouring to remedy the nuisance. The Corporation of St. Helens however . . _ _

were not the only off eacters. The brook received sewage all along. The new asylum at Winwick would tap the brook blfore long with sewage. lie had known the time when.the Corporation of Warrington,from their manure deplit, had tapped it, The Chairman said that when he was the representa• tive of Little Sankey he went to see the works at Long- ford and understood then that the pollution of the brook from that source had ceased.

The Clerk said the smell from the brook was the most constant subject of complaint brought to his notice. The Chairman proposed that the Clerk write to the Corporation upon the matter, and that Mr Halton again bring it before the Rural District Council. Mr Kilshaw seconded. Mr Fulton Smith asked if the Parish Council had not power to bring the matter a little further home than this? Representation on the lines suggested bad been made

before. The Chairman : We have not approached the Cor- poration. • The Clerk said be did not think the Parish Council w,,nld have any power except through the District Council. As private individuals they might have a right of action at common law. Mr Fulton Smith said he believed that if the District Council would not take action they had a right to appeal to the County Council. The Clerk : That is so. The motion was then carried.

div.head: OVERSEERS AND PARISH COUNCIL ACCOUNTS,
div.p: OVERSEERS AND PARISH COUNCIL ACCOUNTS,

The Clerk submitted the over-seers' and Parish Council accounts, which had been audited. He mentioned that the payments of the Parish Council during the year had amounted to £2 9t 21, and there was a balance in band of £1 6s 21. In case of any expenses in connection with the inquiry for the proposed small-pox hospital, they could serve a precept which could be made pay- able upon a 24 hours' notice,
The -accounts were appro; ed. THE PROPOSED SAIALL•PDX HOSPITAL.

A strong complaint regarding the short notice given by the Local Government Board for the inquiry Int 3 the application of the Warrington Corporation for power to borrow money tl erect a small-pox bospitg at Sankey was made by several members. The Council then went Into committee to consider what action should be taken at the inquiry. It was decided that the Council should be represented at te.,-day's inquiry and the objections of the parishioners laid before the Government Inspector.

It used to be a common American Trusts. saying:about our Air °rico

Cousins, that they "wan the earth." The latest developments of the; national characteristic seem to point to the fact that they desire to possess the sea. According 0,1 a Copenhagen telegram 3lr PiERPOINI liloaaalf.s ; Trust has tapped the Scandinavian countries, and it is among the probabilities that the United Steamship Company, with its fleet of over a hum' . dred steamers trading with the United States wit!' shortly be taken over. The recent operations of the Pierpoint 3/forgan "combine" has brought,' within the purview of the people of this conutrf the great Trust question which has so agitated 1 the public mind in America for some years, that two presidential elections took place on the clues" tion as one of the main" planks "in the demo" cratic platform. English people have heard from time to time of " corners " in wheat, iron or cott°3 the work of daring speculators but it has never occurred to us that the whole manufacturing track of America was honey-combed with great combini ations whose sheet anchor is uncontrolled mono- poly. Hitherto the action of these trusts has been confined to the United States, except i 3 the case of a few trades such as manufactured metal goods, where the high prices obtained at home enabied the Americans to flood European-, markets with surplus goods at prices that swept away all opposition. A notable instance was the, Scotch paraffin oil trade which was more than once, placed in imminent danger of extinction by the ‘ competition of the Standard Oil Co. This wealthf, trust,with the:notorious ROCKEFELLER at its head,' tried for over twenty years to extinguish the " Scotch oil trade, and would have succeeded had it not been that the combined stubbornness and in- genuity of the Scotsmen enabled them .to find ways and means of holding out and ultimatelY gaining the victory. The A‘nericans have got, control of nearly all the wells and pipe-lines in the oil-bearing districts of the United States. 13f charging a high price in the States and sending im- perfectly refined oil to this couutry their were able to offer petroleum at lower prices than had ever obtained in Great Britain. Scotch paraffin which at one time brought as much as three shilling per gallon was brought down ill ' a few years to fourpence I At that figure it di& not pay the hatidling either to the Americans or Scotsmen. But the Americans were playing their usual game of losing money to win a big stake', The Scots would have had to close their works they not discovered improved methods of mann' facture, utilised waste materials, and produced $ ' series of by-products which found a ready and 9 profitable market. These brought in a revenue sufficient to ke3p the industry going until the appearance of Russian petroleum in the market, when the Americans withdraw from the competi- tion with largely diminished stocks, and the trade righted itself and came under the legitimate reg""; lation of supply and demand. It is a similar es' perience that is feared by the shipowners of this country,as a result of the PIERPOINT MORGAN COM' bination. It is to be hoped that the issue of the struggle when it comes will be as decidedig in favour of British trade. Ono element ef unfairness in the petroleum competition, it mai be hoped, will not be reproduced in the shipping contest. By a series of commercial le' trigues the government of this country were pre- - vailed upon to admit American petroleum for ' burning purposes to the British market so impel:" fectly refined as to become a positive danger to the community, and although Mr URE, the litember ' for West Lothian has made repeated efforts t° 4 raise the flash-point to a safe standard the publi.ai are still allowed to handle a dangerous foreign O,lr which the makers are forbidden to sell in the!, ~ own country. The ship-owners may at least dsr pend on a patriotic spirit which shall not suffeir ' any such unfair advantage being given to the,,e opponents in the struggle that is likely to to; , place very shortly. Judging from latest reP°riv , they have a stiff fight before them. The Wir, . POINT MORGAN Combination have secured est° ~,. sive ore deposits and steel works in Nova Sco; at Cape Breton and Sidney. This they hope.%o , gis e them a right of exclusion from any datY Viliov might be imposed on American steel. The Welsh Colliery SAD news comes from I • the scene of the recent Disaster. colliery disaster at Ponty- 13ridd. There is no longer any hope of the re- covery alive of any of those still buried in the Workings. Only dead bodies are being brought to the surface and it is hopeless to look for a chance of survival among the remainder. In cases of pit accident by flood or oven black-damp there is always a ground for lingering hope that some 0 the unrescued may be lodged in comparative security in some nook or ledge of the underground Ways. But at Pontypridd the appearance of many of the bodies give indisputable proof that the fire- damp which caused the explosion has also been the nnraediate cause of death; and as the fire is most searching and fatal in its effects the victims still unaccounted for may be given up as lost. The ,aceoes at the pit-head have been of the most heart-rending description, as the remains more or less mutilated were severally iden- tified as the husbands, fathers, sons or brothers, the bread-winners of the hapless throng that ta°ved about in an aimless and distressful fashion ill the neighbolrhood of the catastrophe. The coroner conducts his gruesome investigation from day to day and already the sympathy of the com- munity has found expression in a special relief fund which has been started by the Mayor of Car- With a subscription of £2O. It is well perhaps at a time when a good deal has been appearing it. print derogatory to the miners that attention Should be called to the other side of the question, by a contemplation of the terrible risks which they incur in following their daily vocation. When sPeaking of the high wages sometimes earned by the colliers, people are apt to forget that not only do their wages represent remuneration for a most 3,4trenuous and unwholesome employment, but that iweY cover compensation for dangers which are lal.rainent and constantly present in their daily toil z.nich has been done by legislation to reduce these to a minimum, but they cannot be glttogether eliminated from the pursuit of mining. vi.en where the callous disregard of human life lvcicb used to prevail in such employments has been abolished by means of beneficent legislation there still continues that familiarity with danger Which breeds contempt. This feeling leads to men Playing tricks which the wise reprove, and at which the discreet shake the finger of warning. Unfor- tunately it is not confined to any one set or detachment of the great army of workers that toil in our coal-mines. A miner will discard his safety heep for a naked light, or open his " Davey" to light his pipe, although he knows from the pres- ence of " fire " in the atmosphere of the pit that he does so at the peril of his life and that of his fellow-workers. A fireman going his rounds will omit an insignificaat corner of the workings from his inspection, or a faulty Place from his report. An overseer or manager may from motives of economy in trouble or outlay !ail to strengthen a weak part or to provide just I,e necessary repair, apparatus or supervision, to l'eoP all going in practical safety. It has been Proved on numberless occasions that such practices Pevitably bring disaster in their train sooner or ,4btei% But human nature is week; its memory ia ib'clrt) and the same old mistakes keep repeating ,selves with the sequence of the same sad of t- wl tale of woe. The cause •of the recent acci- -44 le said ta be an explosion of coaldust, but her preventible or otherwise is yet to be ascertained. An heroic glamour has been cast on th e sad event by the gallant conduct of the rescue 'arty who have faced death and danger and in- curred injury before desisting from their fruitless task. It is to be hoped that the hand of benevol- ence will be held open to soothe the anguish and relieve the necessities of the sufferers who remain.

References is being made to the statistics as to the sale of English books on the Continent. It is with s'orne proof of figures, that the name of t Walter Scott is as well known in foreign coun- rles as our own; and when one speaks of the width of Continental taste in literature only a part has been told. In the drama the same catho- -1113 eitY of taste prevails. The performances of Shak- crro's plays are probably more numerous in t.rrnany than in our own country. Every small ,e -"" in the Fatherland is familiar with Hamlet; kld the tale does not end there. It may be said that we, for our part, give Goalie's "Faust " a J.rtain amount of support; but it is very Rht in comparison. In Vienna, for example "le Austrians are familiarised by the drama ii Austrians only with the social life of most `,•:?untries as it is to be seen to-day, but also with Qistorical events which led to the making of tations. We, on the contrary, are content, as a 1111 e, to feast our eyes on musical comedies, with accasional changes to serious and historical drama. utir literature has no doubt gained much from the Nblication of the Tauchnitz editions abroad; but uoth drama and literature have had mainly to de- Pend on translations, and these, luckily, have been ;Lery well done. We must not forget either that ,"ue work has been worth doing well, and has not depended on English idiom for its success.

From 'lle statement which was presented by the Mayor 14,,t the meeting held in the Town Hall on Thursday ;ISt week for the purpose of raising additional funds • aPPears that over £6,000 has been raised for the eral funds which were started shortly after the t29araencement of the war in Smith Africa. Of 4413 amount no less a sum than £4,288 has been 4bacribed for the relief of the wives and children b,sreservists, volunteers aud militia, and only `k) now remains unspent. There are, of °arse substantial balances still in hand on 44erai other accounts,, including those for dows and orphans and other dependents of Ten killed, as well as for the sick, wounded, and eiabled, but these are distinct accounts and can- °t be used for the relief of wivei and children of 135ervi8t5 still in the field. The average weekly ftZl3enditure under this head is £32 and it will • erefore be seen that the existing fund will be ex- to "lasted within a fortnight. It has been decided piornake a further appeal to the employers and ern- • ,Yes of the town for a weekly contribution of £3O I°ng as the war shall last. It is felt that this .:13Peal will meet with a greater share of public 0412Proval than if a large sum were asked for at ,n• In a large town like Warrington there uld be no difficulty in raising £3O for such a worthy object.

The oracle has spoken Mr John Morley made on unursday last week one ofbis all too few visits to the -Ouse of Commons and addressed the assembly. II /4 read of the Rouse being held spell-bound and ten, ing to statements end criticisms from Mr coriey, lips which it would not have tolerated 4°41 any other speaker. The mantle of Mr Glad- w2ne seems ,to have fallen upon his biographer, tau° can claim the attention of the House of Corn- and keep it as no one else could but the Cold Man Mr Morley will never be a adstono , but he is certainly one of the foremost ttrici n the country, a speaker of rare eloquence, th deer), broadminded thinker. His speech on the uoudget was a great one,and undoubtedly raised ate debate to a higher plane that it had reached he arty previous time. Mr Morley's silence has leng bnt he has broken it to excatlent pur- fleti,, In hia criticism he wasted time not on -1.6 of expenditure but at once laid his finger

on the source of the evil to which the Government is hurrying the country. " Policy " was his theme, "the policy which governs expenditure," and in his solemn warning as to the future Mr orley said in effect " You are the little Englanders who are starving social reform and compromising the future of the country iu order to crush the longing for liberty out of the hearts of South African farmers "—a striking indictment which was not without its effect on the listeners and which will be pondered over in the minds of the more thoughtful section of the English people.

The dry weather is rapidly lessening the effi- ciency of drainage both in town and country, and nuisances are becoming prevalent in many places. We carefully refrain from quarrelling with the weather, of course, but the fact remains that sundry well-defined and different stinks are beginning to "talk." The Runcorn Rural Council has a wide and varied experience of this kind of nuisance, and has not yet remedied the one now become famous ab " The Thelwall nuisance." The subject had indeed become distasteful and monotonous to the members, so they would per- haps welcome a complaint at their Tuesday's meeting, which was not from Thelwall. The new nuisance is located at Grappenhall and comes from, the familiar Morris Brook, which Mr R Curran has pushed under the highly-trained nose of the Council for its inspection. There are other unpleasant smells in and around the district, about which people so far have agreed to "grin and bear." One of these is in Latchford Without, and in addition the Ship atrial has begun thus early in the year to emit disagreeable perfumes, which, we understand,even Mr J C Parr complains of though situated two miles away. In • Warrington several of the gridd iver sewers have begun to belch forth sickening fumes, and one of the worst must surely be the one at the bottom of Bewsey-street;which is given a wide berth by those "in the know." The authorities do not appear to make any special effort to alleviate these nuisances and are so far forgetful of their duty that we have labelled a few for their consideration.

div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT. A Provincial Letter.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT. A Provincial Letter.

It is a long time since the various seaside and other health resorts had so good an opportunity of making a golden harvest while the sun shone, as they have enjoyed during the W hitsuntide holi- days. When it is remembered that the last few years have, on the whole, been remarkable for an excess of sunshine and deficiency of rainfall, it is curious at the same time to recall that almost with- out exception the popular holiday seasons were marked by unsettled, and in several cases most un- propitious weather. Indeed, although the Whit- suntide of last year was fairly fine, it was necessary to go back to August 1898 to find a Bank Holiday favoured with the kind of weather condions which have prevailed during the past week. It appears to have been ideal weather all round and every- where, and although the crowds of visitors to the many watering places around the coast may not i have been so large as they are sometimes n August they must have come very near to those numbers. It will interest lovers of cricket to know that Mr Jessop has promised to join Mr MacLaren's team for Australia in the. autumn. Australian cricket, has 'of la e been rather tame and dull, and Mr Jessop will have an oppor, unity of showing the specta- tors that good wickets mean rpportunities of scor- ing at a phenominal rate. There are some cricket experts, however, who do not think this rapid scoring quite right. They cling to the idea that sixty runs an hour is a good pace, and that to ex- ceed it savours of rashness and heterodoxy. It may he so, but if we would be honest there are few who would not admit that when Jessop and his men play to the gallery, the gallery is a very good place to be in.

At lnst we have a "rabbit pest" of our own, and Australia can no longer boast a monopoly of the phenomenon. The plague of rabbits is in full force on ths borders of Dartmoor.. and within easy reacla of a goid market like that of Plymo dth. When it happened at the Antipodes, in the days before cold storage made it poss Ws to send even rabbits to England in marketable con,lition,there was no little wailing over the wa,ts of food-stuff which resulted from the attempts that were made to diminish the number of rabbits, and prevent them eating the farmers out of house and home. Althdugb rabbits are always worth something more than the cost of trapping and st.ooting, they have increased to such an extent on the edges of Dartmoor that they not only take toll of the c ops, but burrow the hedges to such an extent as to cause their destruction and put the farmers to considerable expanse in the way of repairs. to that trappers have r cently ben engaged for the purpose of reducing the pest, and one of them during the pre ent week had no fewer than 144 rabbits as the resul of two night's work in a couple of small fields.

Those who end .avour to spend their holidays so as to be instructive as well as enjoyable do well. This reflection is reproduced every year when one reads of the announcement of where the members of the National Home-Reading Union, propose meeting for their annual holiday. These people do not find it necessary or det.irable to go to Grindel- wald, or some other Swiss retreat, in order success- fully to attain their object. They are content with places within the foil, corners of the United King- dom, and will this year have their outing at Win- chester, which is to be identified with the cele- bration of the millenary of King Alfred's death. The original intention was to make this celebration I one of national importance, but, as with 80 many other well laid schemes, the war in South Africa has interfered so as to upset the arrangement, and the festival will now be restricted within a com- paratively narrow compass. But the members of the Home-Reading Union have deci.ed to obtain all the advantage they can from a stage of Friglish history which may yet teach many important lessons. Hence it is proposed to meet in this ancient city on the 22nd inst., when the Mayor will extend a welcome to the visitors, and we shall be sure to hear more of them. In a somewhat similar way members of the Geological Society have spent their Whitsuntide holdiday in exploring a district em- bracing parr, of South Wales and the neighbouring county of Gloucestershire. Let us trust that while adding to their stores of scientific knowledge they did not fail to thoroughly enjoy themselves.

It was a sad Whitsuntide for the inhabitants of the Aber Valley in South Wales. The terrible colliery disaster had throwii a complete gloom over all the coal district of Glamorganshire and Mon- mouthshire, and sympatty with the families of the victims continues to be a-, genuine as it is wide- spread. Pt common bond is known to unite the whole of the Welsh miners. All underground work- ers are liable to certain risks, and when a disaster like the one that occurred on S iturday morning is reported those above ground instinctively feel that it may be their turn next. The explosion at the 'Universal Colliery was one of the most serious in its results, as it was also the most fierce in its character, that has happened in the Welsh coalfield for some years. The difficulties encountered by the explorers show the terrible force of the explosion and the extensive damage done to the workings, while the loss of life is appalling. Out of eighty- four men at work in the pit only one was brought out alive. All hope was abandoned on Monday of any farther rescue. The cause of the di=aster, will, of course, be officially and strictly inveotigated.

Loss of life is by no mealis uncommon in certain of :he Welsh collieries. A Rises explosion on one occasion cost 145 lives, and on another was account- able for 119 deaths. An accident at Ferndale was responsible for 178 deaths; and the Abercarn dis- aster contributed 268 fatalities. In 1893, 176 lives were lost at Llanerch ; in 1892, 110 were sacrificed at Park Slip, and in 1894, 276 at Ciifvnydd. These are the disasters only in which the loss of life is ex- pressed in three figures. There have been numerous " minor" accidents, all of which at the moment proved painful reminders of the dangerous char- acter of the employment in which many of these underground workers are engaged. The disaster in the Aber Valley has occurred near to the scene of the explosion in June, 1894, which really involved the loss of 281 lives.

--- Every week appears to have its surprise for those who are interested in gas,or the possibilities of the various appliances of electricity, but no one had seemed to think of what might yet be done by re- verting to the use of the ancient oil lamp until the

Kitson light flashed upon a wonder-struck public. From a report issued a few days since by Professor E B Lewes and Mr Boverton Redwood, it was made to appear that the arc lamp and the incandescent gas light were about to meet with a powerful com- petitor in the form of an oil lamp which is said to have been attracting much attention in London. On certain standards which had been erected in the middle of the roadway at Portland Place the lamps are fixed, as an advertisement ; for the latest " new light" comes to us from America. In this so- called Kitson light, ordinary kerosene is gasified under high pressure, and employed to heat a mantle of the ordinary Welsbach type. The report states that the light generated averages 1,000 candles, over extended periods of time; and the inventors claim that the light can be supplied for one-fourth the cost of electricity. " Back to the oil lamps!" may thus become the cry if hal; of what is said of the Kitson light be proved. At present, however, the public will have to do as the story book tells them, " wait for developments."

Support of the Habitual Inebriates' Bill has come from a direction in which the Bishop of Winchester had perhaps not thought to look. Report has it that the Husbands' Protection Society has met in solemn conclave to talk over their wronias at the hands, and possibly claws, of " tyrannical " as well as drunken wives. Anyhow, says the " Chronicle," fourteen sad visaged men again met at St George's Hell, Southwark, when each had a "story to tell." The meeting rejoiced, if these henpecked men can be supposed to have the least feeling of joy in them that the power of the Society had been felt, allud- ing to the clause in the Bill mentioned which would make it possible for a man to obtain a separation from an habitually drunken woman; but curious to relate, they did not pass any resolution!

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY, MAY 31,1901
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, MAY 31,1901
GREAT FIRE AT RUNCORN. ---- Wiggs Works Partially Destroyed. Heavy Damage.

The wont° of Runcorn were aroused from their slum- bers shortly after one o'clock on Saturday morning by the sounding of the fire alarm and the pi olonged hooting of a works buzzer. So prolonged were these sounds that many hundreds came to the conclusion that something more than an ordinary occurrence had taken place and deserted their warm beds and thronged the streets. The news quickly spread that Wiggs works, at the Old Quay the property of the Ignited Alkali Co were on fire and evidence was soon seen in the reflecting sky. Within a few minutes hundreds had assembled in the vicinity of the works, the banks of the Ship Canal, being an admir- able "coign of vantage," and large crowds also assem- bled on Widnes parade,whence they had a splendid view across the broad expanse of the Mersey. For the space of over two hours the fire provided for the spectators a pyrotechnic display such as money would not have pur- chased for them. Wiggs is a very extensive works covering 13 acres of ground and one of the most itnpor- , Cant processes carried out is the manufacture of cyanide of sodium, for which there is a good demand for the purpose of extracting gold from l@w grade errs, which a few years ago were practically worthless under the old method of treatment. The process of manufacture is a patent, discovered within recent years and the "cyanide woiks " at Old Quay, have nat been in exist- ence more than three years. In was in these works that the fire originated and fortunately to those works was It confined,or a conflagration appalling in its destructive- ness would have taken pla e. It appears that about one o'clock on Saturday morn- ing a workman went on a stage near one of the tinnier- , ems towers with which the works abound. To his consternation he found the place on fire to an extent that he could. not cope with it, and he at once gave an , alarm. Luckily the works boasts of a well trained and ' admirably equipped fire brigade, and in a few minutes this had assembled under the command of Mr J Clare. Besides having the Mersey on one side and the Ship Canal on the other, the works have a splendid indepen- dent supply of water at great pressure, and there Is no likely corner of the place where a hydrant is not fixed. In marvellously quick time therefore the brigade were pouring large volumes of water on the burning building. Runcorn Fire Brigade, under Superintendent Wright,were on the spot with commendable promptitude and they were followed at a later period by the Wilders- pool and Warrington Corporation steam fire engine s. It was early evident, however, that nothing but a miracle would save the cyanide works and the workmen and firemen directed their efforts to preventing the fire spreading to the remaining portions of the works. The buildings were of wood, chiefly pitch pine,dry as tinde with the recent hot weather,and with startling rapidityr the flames gained the mastery, and bursting through, the ronf,rose to a great height, and the conflagration could be seen for miles round. As tower after tower collapsed and fell into the fiery furnace of chemicals, sparks flew upwards in myriads and large numbers dropped over a mile away. Oae tower, about 60 feet high, surmounted by an iron tank, created quite a sensation as it toppled over with a great crash. There were several small explosions of chemicals,with- seat power to do much mischief, but a different tale might have had to be told had it not been for the fore- Blest and presence of mind of some workmen. Much used in the manufacture of cyanide is that highly ex- plosive chemical bi-sulphide of carbon. This was stored in a shed on the river side of the works and shortly after the fire waa discovered these men removed the dangerous stuff and deposited it in the Mersey, where it had no power to do harm. Other men boldly undertook the task of ascending a couple of towers and removing the vents' from two tanks of ammonia, so that the liquid could flow harm- lessly away. Had this not been done an upheaval fear- ful to contemplate would have occurred and that some- thing wide reaching in its effects was anticipated, the bellman went round the town warning people to open their windows. The buildings much in danger from the fire were the manure works, recently built at a cost of about £50,000. An easterly wind blew the flames and sparks over these buildings, which were set fire to in numerous places, but a gang of men armed with buckets kept watch on roof, walls and floors, and promptly extinguished any outbreak. The windows of the office were all cracked with the heat, but the building itself was kept clear from serious damage. the workmen and firemen despite the tremendous heat and the clouds of smoke and death-dealing chemical fumes, kept heroically to their task of extinguishing the fire, and only one man was" gassed," a Runcorn fireman, who quickly recovered by the administration of restoratives. By six o'clock the fire bad practically I burnt itself out, and all danger was past. All that was left of the cyanide plant was pines twisted Into all I manner of fantastic shapes, and a confused topsy turvey array of cylinders and tanks, resting upon a smoking, smouldering heap of wreckage. Tee cyanide works were situated right in the heart of the works, which cover thirteen acresrand it is surprising to see standing on either side the large wooden structures common to chemical works, having passed through the fiery ordeal scathless. Mr Fred Norman, the manaeer, was early on , the spot guiding and controlling affairs, and be was joined byofdr J-ereph Morrison, of Widnes, the district , manager, and Dr Rtschen, the chief chemist to tee • Alkali Company. Superintendent Pearson and a staff of constables also rendered valuable services. The value of the building and plant destroyed is roughly , estimated at £20,000, and there was in addition £5,000 worth of stock, which is totally lost. The £25,000 is ' fully covered by insurance. ' The origin of the fire is a complete mystery to all concerned. The plant gave employment to about fifty men,and Mr Norman stated to the press representatives • that these men would not lose their work in consequence of the cstastrophe,as the rebuilding of the works would be proceeded with at tbe earliest possible moment. On . Saturday afternoon the scene of the tlrb was visited by Ms 3 Brock, chairman of the Company, Messrs D McKechnie and Max Muspratt, directors. E Carey, secretary, C Mount, deputy secretary, Dr Clayton, ehemist,and the representatives of the insurance society. Many hundreds of people, impelled by curiosity, also visited the place.

div.head: – _ ST. HELENS FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: - _ ST. HELENS FOOTBALL CLUB.

Annual Meeting. The annual meeting of thoS Elelees Nlrthern Onion Rugby Club was held at the Town Hall on Wednesday night. Mr E J Hannaford was voted to the chair, there being a large attendance. Mr Jfi flolghton. secretary read a letter from Captain Michael Hughes, president, regretting that he was unhble to be present! Mr Houghton then read the annual report. He also read the balance-sheet, by which it appeared that the club had by very carEful management, been lifted clear of debt. In spite of the bad season in the Competition, they had much cause for gratitude, and he felt sure that by careful management the club would go on prospering financially. There had been a large increase in the amount of subscriptions, tbe sum received being the largest in the history of the club—viz., £163 6+ 6i. The president has given a special subscription of £2O to pay the fine in the Liversagl matter. (Applause.) There had been a falling off of £6 in the gate money. The amount paid to players (£321) was an increase of about £36. The team was well supported, and the fact that they tor k the sum of £667 in gate money was a proof that there was still a loyal interest in Rugby football in St.Heleos. He hoped that the coming season would bs a better one all round. Five years ago their liabilities were over £4OO and now those liabilities had disappeared. Mr Houghton then I dealt with the Traynor matter and the circum- stances leading up to Swinton being allowed to transfer him. With the sum so obtained since the balance-sheet was made up, the whole of the £llO liabilities had been cleared off, and for probably the first time in its history the club was out of debt.— On the m3tion of Mr Macdonald, seconded by Mr William Leith, the report and balance-eheet were adopted.—Captain Michael Hughes was re-eleoted president, Mr J U Houghton lion secretary, kad Mr B Jackson, assistant secretary.

div.head: WHITSUNTIDE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: WHITSUNTIDE AT RUNCORN.

Whitsuntide is the great holiday season in Runcorn, and Whit Monday is especially the fete day ot the children. At most of • the works, operations were suspended until Thursday morning and many trades- men closed their shops for alike period. Work was also suspended at the docks for a couple of days. For rhe real enjoyment of a holiday fine weather is essential but unfortunately this brilliant sunshine of the past few weeks gave place to a leaden coloured and a weeping t,ky on Sunday, which is the day when the Primitive Methodists maintain their custom of open air services, but on the present occasion the pilgrimage to Runcorn Bill was dispensed with and the services held in the chapel. Better conditions prevailed on Monday. The early morning was bright and warm, and though later there were occasional dull periods, it was not until well on to four o'clock after the processions bad taken place that a downpour occurred. As usual the procession of

the clnbs took place in the morning and the demonstration was witnessed by large crowds of sight-seers there evidently being many strangers in the town. The Star of Freedom Lodge, G O. Order of Oddfellows, assembled at their headquarters, the Egerton Arms, about nine o'clock, and having been joined in Devon- shire-cquare by the Loyal Order of Ancient Shep'ierds, they led a proemsion through the principal streets of the town to Balton Castle. In front was the Volunteer Band, and next to them Came the officers, viz, marshal, Bro Arthur Grepry ; grand court tylers, Bros T Millington and kbrams ; dispensation carriers, Bros J A Shepherd and Thomas; trustees, Bros Hazlehurst, Findlow and Mather; secre- tary, Bro W Moston ; treasurer, Bro A Shaw; assbtant secretary, Bro W B Jones. The brethren displayed their splendid banner and attractive regalia. From particulars furnished by the secretary it seems that on the Ist January, 1891, the lodge had 230 members, and £4BO in funds, aod 21 juveniles with £7 in funds. There are now 315 members, £1,199 5s 91 in funds, 103 juvenil-s, and £3l 4s 31, in the lodge juvenile brat fhe Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds were accom- panied by the Weston Point Salt _Works Band. At the

front were two guardians (Bros John Jolley and J fi Jolley) attired in ancient shepherd's dress. Neat cana, the officers' in their full regalia, viz. Bros George Williams, WM Thomas Peers, D.M, Arthur Gee, P.M., Daniel Hulse (treasurer), and John Hillidge (secretary.) In the procession there was another shep• herd (Bro Richard Jolley) with dog, and a gaily decora- ted lurry accommodating a shepherd and shepherdess (Bra James Gayter and Miss Elizabeth Ann Hillidge.) This turnout, kindly lent by the Runcorn Co-operative Society, bad a very pretty appearance. Bringing up the rear was the Preston Brook Brass Band. l'he member- ship and finances of the Order are in a satisfactory con- dition. La'cr in the forenoon the officers and members 'of the Upper Mersey Watermen's and Porters' Aisocia- tion paraded the two, about 300 strong. They were preceded by the St. Edward's Catholic Band (Runcorn), and the Association banner. The officers present were : Messrs J Billam (president), J Banner (vice-president), E Gatley (general secretary), T Lee and S Halsworth (branch presidents). The Association was formed in 1889, for the benefit of the flatmen and watcrmen. The porters at Bottom Lacks and the Manchester Warehouse men have since been included, and branch officers established at Runcorn. and also at Manchester.
The afternoon was given up to the processmns of Sunday school scholars. There were three distinct pro- cessions, namely the Church Scholls, the Noncon- formist Schools and the Catholic Schools.

- - ----- The Nonconformist Scholars: assembled at their respective schools and marched to Church-street to join the Brunswick Wesleyan School, which by reason or i's long and honourable history of 100 yeare, took pride of place and led the way. The others followed in the chronological order of their establishment. The route taken was Church-street, Regent-street and Grenway-road to the Park. The 13:uuswick School numbtred 562 scholars, At their head were—are Rev Alfred Wells, Messrs FJ Norman, R Rawlinson, E Taylor, and T Simister (superin- tendents), J Unssvorth, J Birkett, and E Kniveton (secretaries), Next came Sr. John's Presbyterian with 221 scholars. These were preceded by the Rev T Sidney Morris (pastor), Messrs James Pritchard, J Warbur:on (superintendents), R W Harm!), T Dobson, and George Gstley (secretaries). St. Luke's Congregational Mission followed, with 178 scholars. Walking in front were :-.- MCS9TB Slade and Lowe (Fuperintendents), Monsdale (secretary), Tickle (organist), Penny (schoolrnister), Lvdiate, Worrall, and Hailwood. Immediately behind them came Bethesda Congregational led by the Rev J Osborne, Messrs F Beck (superintendent), Scragg and Hayes (deacon.), and J Rate (treasurer). The scholars numbered 193. The Primitive M6thodist School followed next in order with 254 scholars. There were present : Rev W A Eyre (pastor), Mr W H Richardson (superintendent), Messrs James Stubbs, d Hayes, C Hill, R Peacock, H huge, Niekson, Fleet, Ireland, Gittens, and R Lewis. The Halton r ,ad ‘Veslevan (formerly known as Mill-brow Wesleyan) were the next to come in view, having 352 scholars. They displayed their new banner for the first time, and were accompanied by Messrs. S Pope and Findlow (superintendents), J Nall (secretary), J Brown Cornea, Sweetman and Hindley. Following them were the 6cholare of the United Methodist Free Church School numbering 202. These were led by the Rev S Wright (pastor), Messrs J Scragg (superintendent), W Gandy (secretary), M Temperley, T Curzons, Kent, W Booth, Captain Paul, J Holford, W Guy, T Moore, T Povey, E Jones, and W Fowlds. The Camden Wesleyan, as the next in order of seniority, was represented by 422 scholars. The officers present included :—Tne Rev JB- Forster, Messrs S Beckett, and A Harrison (superinten dents), S Littler (secretary), and J Bszley. Nelsen. street Wesleyan School had 158 scholars who were led by the Drum and Fife Band, conducted by Mr Clays. The officials were :—Messrs J Bszley and W Lambert (superintendents), and E Lambert (secretary). The Salvation Army came next with 128 scholars, in charge of Major Spooner, Captain Young and Sergeant Major Jones. Hope Hall Mission brought up the rear with a contingent of 180. They were headed by their new banner, nehind which walked Messrs A Jones (superin- tendent),J T Hughes (secretary), and Messrs Gatley and Bennett (secretaries). .

Throughout the ranks there were numereus banners and bannerettes,and as the procession ilowly wended its way through the streets, the elder sckolars sang hymns. After the procession the Nelson-street Sunday Szbool scholars were entertained to a free tea kindly provided through the munificence of Mesdames F J Nsrman, AR Norman, R U Posnett and J M Frith, which was admir- ably served in the schoolroom by Mesdames Price, Worral and Bazln/ . The Church Schools.

The Parish Church scholars assembled at their head- quarters in Church-street and led off the procession to the stirring music of the Runcorn Velunteer Band. The school was about 1,000 strong. The scholars belonging to Holy Trinity and the Mariners' Mission assembled at the Trinity Sthools and proceeded via High-street and Church-street to Regent-street, to join the Parish Church Schools. Leading the way was the Widnes Subscription Priz Band. The members of the Rev N J Poole's men' Bible class followed, and accompanying the scholars were :—Mrs Killick, Miss Fisher (superintendent of the girls school), Mr G W Gibson, superintendent, and Mr W a Leathwood (of the Marines's Mission School), and the teachers. There were between 600 and 700 scholars In the procession. The Mill Brow Ragged School came immediately behind, in charge of Mr W J Cunningham (superinteprlent). and Mr James Wilding. There would be about ZOO scholars in this contingent. Next in order of procession came the St Michael's school, also displaying a brilliant regalia. They were accompanied by the St Mary's Prize Band from VVidnes. The number of scholars present was 282, and there were in addition 50 members of a juvenile Bible class. When the pre cession reache Devonshire-square the Mersey Mission school filed up behind Sc Michael's and thus completed the demonstration of the Church Schools. Leading the Mission School was the hand of the Weston Salt Works. Prior to joining the other schools there had been two interesting functions performed in con- nection with the Seamen's Institute. These were the opening by Miss Digges of the new recreation ground and bowling alley rectntly constructed on land adjoin- ing the Institute. During the procession the scholars were 318 strong. The route taken by the combined procession was Regent-street, High-streat, Bridgc-street Mill-brow. Victoria-road, and Greenway-road. On the way the Trinity,Mariners and Mill-brow schools dropped out and proceeded to their respective fields for recrea- tion. The Mersey Mission School left tbe Parish Church and St Michael's in Greenway-road and after paying Mr R Abel a visit at Crofton Lodge they repaired to the recreation ground in the Holloway. rhe Parish Church and St Michael's Schools, proceeded according to cus- tom to the Vicarage, and were drawn up on thp. lawn to sing the National Anthem. They ware there joined by the Weston (8t John the Evangelist's) school. This dependency of the Parish Church fur- -1 i ihed an attractive spectacle. The Catholic School.

The St. E I wards Catholic School paraded the town separately to the strains of their own brass band in smart new uniform. They were about 306. Lead''lg the waY were the Rev Father Chambers (priest-in- charge), the Very Rev Dan Lynch (Chester), and the Rev Father Roach (Knutsford), Considerable ettention had been bestowed upon the attire of the scholars, the guts being costumed in white gowns with red and blue sashes, and the boys in white suits with yellow sashes. These represented respectively the confraternity of the Children of Mary and the Sacred Heart. The scholars also carried miniature poleE festooned with a variety of blooms. Their general get-up was greatly admired as the procession moved along the streets. The school children were regaled with tea at their respective 'schools later in the afternoon, and in several cases the feast was followed by an entertainment. Tax GLEN-Sens. div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
COLONEL WRIGHT AT RUNCORN.

At the Salvation Army Barracks, Runc-orn,next Sunday night, Colonel Ted Wright will attend and preach. The service begins at 645 pm, and all are invited. Colonel Wright is a native of Runcorn, and a forcible preacher A SAILOUS' PAILTY.

A party of sailors numbering about BO were hos- pitably entertained by MrSmythe. of Barrow Wood Hall, near Tarvin, on Wednesday last. fhe sailors, who were under the 'care of the Rev E Lambert senior chaplain, of the Mersey Mission, were from the several institutes at Liverpool, Bootle, Birken- head, Garston, Ellesmere Port and Runcorn. The Runcorn contingent numbered eleven and were ac- companied by Mr W Shaw Missionary. WHIT MONDAY REVELLERS. Annie Griffiths and Elizabeth Barker, pedlars, were charged at Runcorn Police Court on Tuesday with being drunk and disorderly. On Whit Mon- day the prisoners were sitting on the door step of the house of Mr Cooke, relieving officer. They were very drunk and were smoking short clay pipes and drinking ale from a bottle. Barker was singing " Drinking at the fountain." PS Gregory and P.O Wilding apprehended the prisoners who were each fined 58 and costs 53 or seven days. Their licenses were endorsed.

MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN'. The annual excursion to Liverpool and New Brighton took place on Tuesday and was a success. The saloon steamer Snowdrop had been chartered, and the trip down the Ship Canal and river was highly enjoyed by 800 passengers. Music was sup- plied by the Salt Uaion Brass Band and Mr C Tanks String Eaud. The weather was delightfully fine and a happy day was spsnt amid the manifold attractions of the seaport city and New Brighton. The return voyage was safely accomplished in good time.

div.head: ALLEGED THEFT OF` CLOTHING.
div.p: ALLEGED THEFT OF` CLOTHING.

At Runcorn Police Court on W;i-i-i-e-day Lillie Draper. aged 13, years, was charged with stealing a towel and various articles of underclothing from the house of Margaret Ellison, wife of a waterman 45. Ashbridge-street. The prosecutrix said the prisoner's father's house was next door. Since February she had continually missed things from er the house. Last Saturday suspicion rested upon the prison because she was wearing some of the stolen articles. P.S Gregory spoke to apprehend- iug the prisoner, who admitted her quilt. She was remanded until Monday and set at liberty on bail. THE CHARGE AGAINST A WiDNES OFFICIAL.— FURTHER REMAND. At Widnes Petty Sessions, yesterday morning, John Drury, of Ditton, late assistant collector to the Widnes Corporation, was brought up on remand charged with the alleged embezzle- ment of .£596 16s Id, the moneys of his employers, the Corporation.—Mr Watkin Oppen- heim, for the Corporation, said that a further remand until Monday was necessary. He under- stood that one of the" bail " had not turned up, and he asked the defendants other bail if he would stand for the £lOO. He consented to do so, but there was some doubt at to his being able to cover that amount in case of necessity. Defendant Was allowed a few hours whereby to find the remaining .E5O. The case stands over until Monday. Drury was admitted to bail, himself in one surety of £lOO and two others in £5O each.

ALLEGED THEFT FROM A BOAX AT RUNCORN. At the Runcorn Police Court, on Saturday,before Mr SO Win Imison, Joseph Yates, a boatman, was charged with stealing three windlasses and a pair of leggings, the property of James Sandbaclr—Mary Ann Sandbach. wife of the prosecutor, stated that she lived at 27, Canal-street. Her husband was a batman, and had charge of the Fannie and the Pink belonging to Mr: Jonathan Eforsefield. The prisoner had been Working with them as mate, and they had been paying him 8s for the trip from Run- corn to Altrincham. The windlasses belonged to the prosecutor, but elle could only identify one of them which had had a piece knocked out of it, The leggings also belonged to her husband. She missed them at the bottom of the Manchester Lock.—Ser- geant Gregory stated that he found the windlasses on the boat Kate at Weston Point on the previous Pinki.l—The was andeo e h: rrgeemd.—gvidence was given until Tuesday, day. The leggings were found on board the boat Th by William Robson,captain of the Kate, that he had had the windlasses in his possession two years,hav- ing found them in the canal at Manchester.—The prisoner was discharged. Early on FARm Sunday FIRE morning T Tt li a h broke out on a t small farm situate in Sea-lane,Halton, in the occup- ation of John Tomlinson. A messenger was des- patched to Runcorn, and the Yin Brigade were I warned, but before theyßEc o flames had got a firm hold of the buildings. There was a strong breeze blowing at the time, and this materially assisted in the spread of the conflagra- tion. So readily did the woodwork yield to the could Na reach fire . 10 place the flames that it was impossible to rescue some 27 geese and fowls and these perished. The brigade turned out smartly, only to find, however that the fire was beyond them, and the buildings were practically burned to the ground. Besides the poultry, a quantity of harness, ploughing gear, cart sheets, hay and straw provender, and farm imple- ments were destroyed, the estimated damage being .£l3O. This is happily covered by insurance. The i farm s close by the Bridgewater Canal and it is supposed that a spark from one of the steam tugs plying between Runcorn and Manchester ignited the buildings which had been rendered in a com- bustible condition owing to the recent spell of dry weather. Although the brigade were unable to save the stock Sr.c., they rendered timely assistance in keeping the fire within bounds.

EARLICBTOWN WEIBLWRIGIITB PICNIC. On Saturday afternoon, a number of the wheel wrights employed at the Viaduct Works had a jaunt as far as Abbey Lakes. Leaving Earlestown in a wagonette about one o'clock they had an en- joyable drive taking with them as a guest, Nfr J Sin4leton, who for 42 years has been employed at the works as a wheelwright, and has recently re- tired on a pension. On arrival at the Lakes a game of bowls was played, and after tea, Nir Singleton was presented with an ebony walking stick, as a mark of esteem.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[Blt A CORRESPONDENT.]

The &lief event of the week has been the fire at Wiggs Chemical Works. I had not the good for- tune to see the blaze—rising in the wee sma hours is not one of my good qualities—but those who were there described the seene as magnificent. There certainly should be something splendid for an expenditure of £25,000, but I dareqty that the United Alkali Company think the money was well worth the display. An old stager however, tells me that it did not approach, let alone rival, the fire at Runcorn old soapery, when there were literally rivers of burning oil.

Saturday's outbreak might easily have been far more disastrous in its results. There might have been an explosion which would have devastated a wide area and claimed many human victims, and not only the Alkali Company and the Insurance Company, but the people of Runcorn ought to be thankful to the men who by their forethought and pluck averted such a disaster. Little did many thousands of us know when we arose on Saturday morning, never even having heard the buzzer, how narrowly we had escaped being "blown up." Bad as the fire was it might have been worse and it is satisfactory to have Mr Norman's avowal that no men will be thrown out of employment.

This is the second Whitsuntide holiday Mr Nor- man has had snatched from him as it were. Twelve months ago he had arranged to spend several days away from home. Boxes were packed and waiting in the hall ready to be conveyed to toe station, when an explosiou occurred at the cyanide plant and a man was killed. Departure therefore was utterly out of question. Last Saturday forenoon he intended to seek fresh woods and pastures new, but instead he is called to the Works in the middle of the night and spends many weary hours of harassing, enervating toil fighting fire's relentless sway, and his whole Whitsuntide unravelling the consequent tangle produced by the destruction of the works. Hard lines, isn't it? Mr Norman has done much to retain and extend the industries at Old Quay, and it is regrettable that such a misfor- tune as this serious fire should have interrupted his plats.

It was amusing during the scholars procession on Monday afternoon to hear the remarks passed in the higher portions of Greenway-road. The banner of Brunswick Wesleyan School first appeared in sight, iith the leading lights of Wesleyanism im- mediately behind. The Church Schools have usually led the way at this point, and the cry repeated again was "where's the Churcti"?As Nonconformist School after Nonconformist School passed along, the query was continually repeated, "wherever can the Church be," and it was evident that the idea of the Church Schools coming in at the tail end of the procession was not palatable. At length the long line of Dissenters passed and then after a short break, the Parish Church and other schools came on the scene. It appears the Church procession was too late coming along Victoria-road to take prece- dence of the Nonconformist Scholars, who marched by way of Greenway-road anti naturally finding the way clear, went straight ahead. A very simple ex- planation of an iec.dent which has given rise to considerable discussion.

div.head: AN INGENIOUS SWINDLER. --- How Warrington Women were Victimised.
div.p: AN INGENIOUS SWINDLER. --- How Warrington Women were Victimised.
An All Fools Day Escapade.

The ingenious manner in which a number of Warrington women have been gulled into parting with some of their money to an imposter, was re- vealed at the County Borough Police Court on Thursday. A young man of respectable appearance, named Thomas Monks, residing in Robson-s.treet, Warrington, was placed in the dock and cbarged with stealing from the dwelling-house of Rachael Hayes, f 37, Lythgoes-lane, a man's jacket and muffler, value Os. the property of James Hayes. He was further charged with obtaining money by means of false pretences from Helen Moory, 4, Dickenson-stteet,and Catherine Alice Hill, 3. Thel- wall-laner Mr T S Steel appeared on behalf of the prisoner and.pleaded guilty to all the charges. At the outset the Chief Constable explained that he couldshave preferred eight charges against the prisoner but as it was usual to go into three only he had selected the three most serious cases. The pro- secutor in the first case was a spinner living at 97, Lythgoes-lane, and six wedge ago, the prisoner came to lodge at the house. He stayed there about a week and on April 223 d disappeared without going through the slight formality of paying for his lodgings. Subsequent to his departure the clothing mentioned in the charge was missed. When appre- hended at Manchester by Superiatendent Monaghan, prisoner was fou-id to be wearing the stolen articles. Referring to the second charge, Mr Talbot said that at 10 o'clock on Monday morning, April Ist (a very appropriate day for the transaction) prisoner went to Mrs Moory, woo lived at 4, Dickenson-street, and handed her a note purporting to be written by her hus- band who was at work. The tenor of it wag " Give the bearer the sum of 53. Mr Moss (his employer)is not in. R.Moory." The woman gave him 53 and he went away. An hour later he returned and pre- sented a second note, saying that it was not 5s which her husband wanted but 103. Mrs Moory bad not the exact sum of 5s so she gave him 4s so, making a total ot 9, sd. When her husband returned home in the evening he said he knew nothing about the note and he had not authorised anyone to ask for money. Mr and Mrs Moory were only poor working people, in fact all the people who had been affected by the man's de- predations were of the working class. With regard to the third ease the prisoner obtained LI from Mrs Rill, Thelwall-lane, on April Ist. He turned up in the course of the day with a note said to be from Mr Rill, reading something like this :—" Give bearer 10s as Mr Hughes, our cashier is not in, and it Is very urgent." The amount mentioned in the note was very indistinct but Mrs Hill went and changed a sove- reign and gave the prisoner be. Subs-quently he returned with a second note stating You mis- understood me. It was a sovereign I wanted not 103, give bearer a few coppers too" Mrs Hill gave the prisoner another 10s and he went away saving " I shall have to be sharp and get back before Mr Billington comes in or I shall be sacked." Mr Billington was a foreman at Messrs Richmond's' where Mr Rill was employed. When Mr BM came home it was found that the prisoner was an impostor. Infor- mation was given to the police and prisoner had been identified in that and a great many other similar cases

A specimen of the note which the prisoner produced was handed up for the inspection of the Bench, the Chief Constable Stating that it was written in the ordinary schoolboy handwriting, largely adopted by workingmen, There was no wonder at the women Ix ing deceived, not having seen their husband's writing inece the days of the love letters. (Laughter.) The police had been searching ior the man very diligently for many months, and he was arrested on coming out of Strange- ways gaol on TuPsday. He had been very 111 since his apprehension, and had ben under the care of the Police Surgeon. He was apparently in a very nervous state, and appeared to feel his position acutely. Mr Meaty called arid in answettollfr Steel said he had known the prisoner for some time and had found him to be a respectable young man. Mr. Steel then addressed the Court for the defence.

He desired to lay a few facts before the magistrates in the hope that they would see their way to deal leniently with the prisoner. With regard to the larceny, prisoner was lodging at Mrs Hayes' and on the morning mentioned had to go to Bolton to collect some money that was owing to him. His own coat had been pawned and another mao who was lodging there offered to lend him his coat. Prisoner tried it on but it did not fit and the lodger then told him to take the coat mentioned in the charge but to bring it back again. He took it away and of course that cons'it uteri larceny. 1 The Ch ef Constable: The other man absolutely denies that. Continuing Mr Steel said, the prisoner was twenty four years of age and prior to this,had had a very good character indeed. For ten years he worked at Messrs Richmond and Co.'s works as a moulder and had never lost a minute at his work. Be saved up £.50 and bought some furniture witb the object of getting married lotit unfortunately he lost Lis work at Richmond's and got into the company or certain betting people in this ;own. They took him to their house and spent the nights in playing cards and dominces, and undoubtedly " fleeced " the prisoner. Still more unfortunately three years ago be was seized with an epileptic fit, and since that time hal been subject to them At times he had no control °Nur his feelings, and he did not know what possessed him to take the money. Some twelve months ago he,attempted to drown himself at Howley. Be was taken to the Wsrkhouse hospital and remained there 14 days. After that he attempted to poison him- self. He had been in prison, and during that time again attempted to poison himself. There were other charges against the man, and he asked si the Bench to take that into consideration. Judges had often said that charges ougbt to he amal- gamated and one punishment inlSicted for all. He asked the magistrates to deal as leniently as possible with the prisoner. He was in a State of impaired health and would have been brought before the court the previous Iday but he was in fits for two hours. He (Mr Steel). submitted that it was owing to the man's weakened intellect and loss of money in gambling that lie occupied
that position. He also pointed that he knew the persons to whom be went for the money. . . . _
The Chief C listaVe said the prisoner had been living on the money obtained in this way for mouths. Tle was wanted .at.many places for similar offences.

The Chairmar; (Mr J Hepherd) said it was a very painful case ta deal with. Tney were very Barry te see the prisoner in that position but the offences with which he was charged were sa serious that they could not be overlooked. He would have to go to gaol for a mouth on each charge (three months in all).

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
THE ROTS AND THE RABBIT-A GIRL'S DETECTIVE INSTINCT.

the Warrington Police Court on Friday, before the Mayor and other magistrates, Thornas Davies, 11, zabeth-Areet, and Jarvies Taylor, 2, Back Haydock- street, boys aged twelve years, were charged with stealing a tame rabbit, valued 5s the property of John Whitny, from a hutch at 10, Llanover-street.—They plealled guilty—The Chief Constable stated that the prisoners had been living a loose life for some time. At ten o'clock on Thursday night they went by tLe back way to Mr Wintny's house and asked for a drink of water. They were sup- plied by Elith Whitney, prosecotoi4s daughter, and weut away. In the back yard there Was a hutch occu- pied by a tame rabbit. At seven o'clock that (Friday) merning, the door of the hutch WM found wide open and the rabbit was missing. The girl, who seemed to have a detective instinct, went to several dealers to see "

if her pet had been sold in boadage. (Laughter). At Locker'a establishment in Mil-street, she found the Ptiaoners. She noticed that their coats were covered with hair, which she rec.agniz ad as the natural colour of the rabbit. She accused the boys of the theft and they denied it, but the rabbit was found In a hamper near them. The prisoners were detained until the arrival of P.S. Hfflingworth, and ultimately they admitted stealing the rabbit. Both prisoners had been before the Court several times pre- viously:—The Bench decided to send the boys to a refor- matory for five yearer. A BEGGING IMPOSTOR SMARTLY CAVORT. at the County Bordner) Court on Whit Monday,belore Mr F Monks and other magistrates. John Hallam, who described himself as a cycle maker, of Manchester, was charged with begging in Bridge-street on Saturday. He pleaded not guilty.—Detecti ye Superintendent Monaghan said that about four o'clock on Saturday afternoon be was in Hots 'market-street and sa., the prisoner with a little girl. his hands were bandaged and one was in a sling. Be saw him ask for b;1119 and hearrThim tell a pitiful tale. He shook as though he was afflicted with St Vitus's dance. Witness afterwards saw him with 1 a little boy and questioned him about his c-implaint. Prisoner told him that hid injuries were very painful indeed. Witness bad his suvicions and ultimately had the man brough: to the Police Station. There the bandages were taken off. Prisoner pretmded to suffer the greatest pain and it took three men to hold him. The bandages off, ir Was found that there was nothing the matter with him. The police surgeon afterw ,rds examined the man and c rtified as follows : —" I found an old injury which perhaps has been done for years but there is nothing recent and nothing to prevent his working. He was suffering from the effects of drink." Questioned by witness, prisoner said he had been in the Liverpool Infirmary, but when it was suggested that intl.:ides would be made he acknowledged that he put the bandages rrund his hands himeelf, He was the cleverest impostor witness bad ever come across. The Chief Con-table said the prisoser was a very vfgerotis, sturdy, lusty little man and a very impudent one.—Prisoner said he was a cycle maker by trade but had received several injuries and could not follow his emnloyment. Ha obtained some work lest week at the Liverpool dock., and was walking to Warrington en Friday when he was robbed of Hi. Be gave informa- tion .0 the pelice at Warrington and when he was asked to go to the Police Station he thought it was to five a description of the man who had robbed him. He denied that he had asked for alms or that he had any need to do so. The police officer came to him while he was in the lodging houso.—The Chief Constable: The Super- intendent was never near the lodging house. Prisoner I had no need to beg. I had paid my lodgings, rile Magistrates sent prisoner to goal for one month. Pris- oner: A month' What for ? The Chairman : Because you are a rogue and a vagabond,
