div.p: MINOR OASES.
Warrington Borough Court.

FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair) Coutteillor Smethurst and Mr Thornton. AN UNPROVoKED AS3AULT.--WilliaM turley was sum- moned for assaulting John William Howard, 18. Foundry- street on the 18th inst. Defendant did not appear. Com- plainant stated that he met Curley in Bewsey-street, and without any provocation he struck him. He had not seen the man since. Defendant Who had been before the court 17 times was fluid 104 and costs. BEEN AFTER TEA AND THE REM:LT.—William rilley was summoned for assaulting Florence Riley, his aunt, living at 16 Gough's yard, on the 19th Inst. Complainant said that on Sunday afternoon she and the defendant and some oth.r rel.tlvee went for a walk and afterwards had tea together. After tea they had some beer and at nine o'clock defendant became quarrelsome and wanted to fight his brother. Wit- ness interfered and he struck her.—Defendant alleged that Complainant was the aggressor. The Mayor said it seemed as if the affair was the result of having beer on the top of tea. Defendant would be fined 25 6d. MolSDlY.—Before Mr F Monks (in the chair), and Messrs John Fairclough. Hayward and Thornton. THEFT OF A BOY'S et:Fr.—Thomas Warburton, 64. Sharpe- street, was charged with stealing from outside the shop of Messrs Calvert Bros., Orford-lane, on Saturday night a boy's suit valued at ls ed.— The Chief Constable said the prisoner was seen by a young lady to take the suit, put it under his coat and walk away. She informe4 the shop manager and he followed the prisoner. but could not catch him up Infor- mation was given to the police. P.C. Dyson searched the neighbourhood and found the prisoner near the C. L C. rail- way embankment—Prisoner who pleaded guilty. vros sent to gaol for a month. Mfactuzasgotra.—Thomas Glynn. last from Wigan, was charged with having been drunk at half-past twelve on Sun- day morning. The Chief Constable said he was a harmless ii,rt of character, and was locked up more for his own safety than anything else. He was discharged—Joseph Webb was charged with sleeping in an out building in Earle-street on Saturday night. He was discharged with a caution.—John Newnes, 88. Cburch-street, was fined 5s and costs for having been drunk and disorderly in Church-street on Sunday might. TUESDAT.—Before Alderman Shaw Green (in the chair) and Dr. Fox. I.I6EFULNESS OF AMBULANCE PoLICEMEN.—MichaeI . Murray. et Silver-street (who now made his 10th appearance before the magistrates) was ch*rgeri with being drunk in Buttermarket-street, on the 19th May. PC. Hurst proved the case, and said the men was exceedingly drunk and was Lying on the footpath suffering from a wound at the back of head. He was conveyed to the police station on an ambul- ance. They had to get a great quantity of drink off his stomach before they could bring him round. The Chief Constable, " It was a good thing for him that there are such beings as ambulance policemen." Fined 5s and cc sts. TILE LODOND AND His Doo.—Richard Hinton, 2, Lyon- street, was charged with keeping a dog without a licence on the 19th May.—Deienndant pleaded guilty •• in one sense." —The Clerk What sense is that ? —Defendant : Toe dog be- longs to a man who used to lodge with me. He has gone away and left it.—Defendant admitted that he vine in charge of the animal, and the Clerk ruled that he was therefore responsible.—P 0 Hardy proved the case, and the defendant was tined is 6d. P.3LICE ANNAULTED.—A. "'ARM LABODRER'e Jona mansaton. a farm labourer, woe charged with bar.
iviiii

been drunk and disorderly In Bridge-street at 2.45 on Monday afternoon and assaulting P.O. Heap and P.O Bruen.—P.C. Heap said he was on duty in Bridge-street when he was called to the Royal Oak public-house to eject prisoner and another man. They both went out When, requested but when they got outside the prisoner said he would not go away for any "copper," big or little ; but would please himself where he went. He was very violent on the way to the Pollee Station and witness had to obtain the assistance of P.C. Bruen. As they were entering Mersey- street prisoner tripped P.C. Bruen and when he was on the groond kicked him on the thigh. He then kicked witness on the leg. They had great difficulty In taking him to the Police Station.—Prisoner was fined 63 and costs for being drunk and disorderly and was sent to goal for 21 days for the assaults.

AN UNLICENSED Can DRIVER.—Peter Wilson was charged I with having on the 22nd Mayacted as the driver of a hackney I carriage without a lieense.—lnspector Taylor, inspector of Warrington hackney carriages, said that he was in Bridge- street' on the day in question when he saw the defendant in charge of a cab. He was not a liCenied driver, and the vehicle belonged to his brother Arthur. Witness did not speak to him then about the matter, but he had done se on previous occasions, and warned him about the offence he was committing. His excuse generally was "I have only just come up to take the cab off Jenks" (the regular driver). ihe defendant had no right to use the cab. He was however, a very good driver and a very good man. P.O Baxendale saii the defendant was la charge of the cab an hour and five minutes to his knowledge. A fine of 5s was infUcted, and the Chairman rec Dr/mended the defendant to take out a licence. He had rendered himself liable to a penalty of 40s and costs. _

A NIGHT SCENE IN RICHARDSON'S ROW.—Mary Fisher, wife of John Fisher, of Pye's-yard. was charged with having been drunk and disorderly on the 21st May in Richardson's- row —P.C. Woods said that on the night in question the defendant created a disturbance outside the house in which her husband was staying from 9.15 to midnight. The langu- age she used was of an obscene character and could be heard all over the neighbourhood. Many of the neighbours corn plained about her bad conduct. She was not living with her husband, they had separated by mutual consent. The woman was drunk.—The Chief Constable Inform.d the Bench that there had been three previtus convictions against the defendant for drunken and disorderly conduct —She was fined lOs and costs. altogether 21 Is. WOMEN PUGILISTS—Sophia Madigan and Catherine Todd, both living at 314. Kautsford-road were, on the evidence of Sergeant Bvans, bound over to keep the peace for fighting in linutsford-road on the 17th May, and also ordered to pay the costs.

div.head: Daresbury Petty Sessions.
div.p: Daresbury Petty Sessions.

TUESDAY.—Before Mr Meld (in the chair) and Messrs Tinsley, Frost, Talbot, Knowles and Edelsten. TRESPASSERS oN THE APPLETON RESERVOIR.—Mr Stanley Wilson, deputy town clerk of Warrington, mentioned the case against John Crocker, William Hamblett and Albert Taylor who were summoned for trespassing on the embank- ment of the Corporation reservoir at Appleton. The appli- cation, he said, was for permission to withdraw the summons against the defendants, as they had expressed their regret, promised not to repeat the offence and paid the costs. The only object the Corporation had in taking the proceedings was to let the public know that they were determined to put a stop to the constant damage done by trespassers on the embankment of the reservoir. The Bench acceded to the request, and the cases were accordingly withdrawn. THE MUZZLING oF DoGa.—Ebenezer England, Whltefield- rosd, Stockton Heath. was summoned for allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled and without collar at Walton on May 10th. Mr England explained that his daughter took the dog out. Its collar was than on. At Walton she no iced that the collar was missing and turned back to look for it when she met the police officer —The Chairman said a technizal offence had been committed and a fine of 3s 61 would be imposed.—Frederick Hathbone, Stockton Heath, was similarly fined for allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled and without collar at Stock- ton Heath on May 16th,—Ralph Clarke, d rappenhad, was summoned for a similar offenee at irappenhall on May 22nd. Ho stated that the dose was on the doorstep of the house and that the land for some little distance ia front was private. The police officer said he saw the dog on the bridge. WO yards away from the house. A fine of 3s 6d was imposed.— The Police Superintendent said they did not want the muzzling order in Cheshire. It was only by strictly carry- ing out present regulations that they would be able to do without it.—Elijah Leslie, carter, WArrington, was fined 3s 6d for a similar offence at Grappenhall on May 22nd,

div.head: Sankey School Board
div.p: Sankey School Board

The monthly meeting of the Great Sankey School Board was held at the schools on Tuesday evening, Mr Halton presiding, and there were also present Messrs It Perks, Bilshaw, Fulton Smith. and W D. Jeans jun, (clerk).—The headmaster (Mr 6 Clarke) introduced the question of the slimmer holidays. Ile said the majority of the schools in Warrington had been closed owing to an epidemic of measles. It was thought advisable in Warrington to close the schools on the third week in July instead of the last week in June. He thought it would be advisable for the Board to state whether they would fall in with the arrangement at the Warrington schools or have their holidays at the usual time.— Considerable discussion took place and eventually the chairman moved that the holidays take place as usual, commencing on the Thursday before Walking Day.—Mr Halton moved that the matter be left in the hands of Messrs Perks and Fulton Smith to consider and decide upon.—Mr Perks thought it would be better to settle the dispute at , the present meeting. He proposed that they have ' the holidays at the same time as the schools in Warrington.—Mr Kiishaw seconded, and the motion met with the approval of the Board.—lt was also decided to allow the school to break up on the Wednesday afternoon previous to Walking Day.

Fatal Result of a Fall. The death took place at 5.30 on Monday morn- ing of Mary Antwiss (69). wife of James Antwiss, of 7, Paradise-place. Ihe deceased had been in a feeble Condition for two years, and at 10 o'clock on the morning of the 21st mat, a neighbour visited her for the purpose of supplying her with food And than left the hou4e. On returning in about five minutes' she found deceased lying on the back kitchen floor. It was evident that she had been seriously injured, and Dr smith was sent for, and I found that Mrs Antwiss was suffering from a broken thigh. Re attended her until her death,_ An inquest was held by Mr. Brighouse at the Police Station on Wednesday evening. Evidence was given by Mr. James Antwiss, husband of the deceased and Mrs Barlow, of 6, Paradise Place bearing out the above facts,—A verdict of 'Accidental Death "was returned.

div.head: WARRINGTON RELIEF FUND EXHAUSTED. – Public Meeting in the Town Hall.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON RELIEF FUND EXHAUSTED. - Public Meeting in the Town Hall.

A Further Appeal to be Issued. In consequence of the funds subscribed for the relief of the wives and children of reservists being almost exhausted, a public meeting was held in the Town Hall Warrington for the purpose of raising further funds for preserving the homes of the men serving their country in S-uth Africa and for helping their wives snd children. Ti,e Mayor (Alderman Roberts) presided and there were also present: Alderman Fairclough (deputy Mayor), Councillor Burton,CMonel Ridgway, Messrs T H Cook, Wilcock, Dallow, Ribber, Pearson, with J Lyon Whittle (town clerk), 9 Wilson (deputy town clerk),and William Boyle (Borough Treasurer's Department.) . .

The Mav-ott said he-thought he could introduce the business by saying that practicallly the object for which they had met was oce of which they had been kept fully acquainted from week to week and it would be interesting no doubt to have put before them the figures up-to-date in connection with the subscriptions received and their distribution. He regretted, as they all regretted, that the long and quite unexpected duration of the war had made it necessary to make a further appeal for help. None of them imagined for a moment when, fifteen months ago, they issued an appeal which was so splendidly responded co and which came as a surprise to them all, that it would be necessary to make a further appeal, and in fact a third appeal,as the present one was. He wished to impress this fact upon them ',hat their obligation to the men at the front had increased rather than diminished owing to the long duration of the war. When they remembered that the first contingent of Warrington Volunteers were only now returning after 15 months absence and that their places had to be taken by a further section, it brought home vividly to those who had bad the pleasure of staying at home in comparative comfort and even luxury, the patriotism, determination. Pluck and endurance, and iu all cases of personal bravery when called upon, of the men who had borne the brunt of the battle. Therefore their responsibility to those whom these men had left behind and whom the townspeople undertook should not suffer—not simply the wives of volunteers but also of reservists and militiamen—had not diminished but had xtended. How long the war was going to last no one could tell but he thought he should be able to put before them figures which would show that the demands upon them were not beyund the capacity of the town. Before going further be ought to state that he had reeived a letter from Mr Milner of the Whitecross Company who stated that the firm would take notice from the figures sub- mitted at the meeting what was required, and would do their part towards that patriotic cbject• He (the Mayor) had also to apologise for the absence of the Rev John Yonge whp waa:engaged in connection with church work, and he had also received a letter front Colonel Fitzherbert, who said he regretted that an attack of bronchitis following influenza would preterit him from attending the meeting. He was entirely in sympathy with the object, and was willing to act on any commit., tee on which his services would be useful He (the Mayor had also to apologise for the absence of Major Booms and Mr Hibbert bad just handed to him a letter from Mr Ziba Armitage in which he stated that he and his directors had decided to make a further contribution to the fund of £2O. (Hear. hear). The financial posi- tion of the fund was as follows :—Total amount of subscriptions for WiVPR and de- pendents of reservists including £153 19s 51 originally subscribed for Transvaal refugees and which had been used for the wives and dependents of reservists, £4,288 23 lid ; widows and orphans and other dependents of men killed, £1,280 19s 6d :sick wounded and disabled, £25.1. 17s 7d. To these subscrip- tions must be added the balance of the School Girls Bazaar fund, £202 9. 21 ; and subscriptions received in connection with the departure of the third contingent of volunteers amounting to £32 09 6d, making a grand total of £6,058 9s Bd. The expenditure had been as follows :—Allowances to wives and other dependents of reservists, volunteers, and militia £3,859 103 7d, temporary allowances to widows, &c £lO2 5s 10d, allowances to dependents of men invalided £9 14s id, printing and advertising £222 3r 7d, postages and petty expenses £2O Us, renewal of volunteer assurances (first contingent), field glasses, and insurance of third centingent £216 83 6chtotal £4,430 133 7d. This left a balance in hand of £1,425 6s 11d, in addition to the balance on the school girls bszaar fund account of £202 9s 21. Of that sum £1,280 19s 61 was ear-marked for widows and orphans and other depen- dents of men killed, and £254 17s 'id for sick, wounded and disabled. The only balance available for reser- vis.s' wives, after charging deficiency on Volunteer account and proportion of advertising and expensee,and setting aside the School Girls Fund was one of £6O. They had in band a further sum of £232 in con- nection with the Volunteer Reception Account but that wasa distinct matter. Since the commencement of the fund 195 wives, 353 children and 111 other dependents had been assisted. This number had been reduced in consequence of the return of some of the men and there were now in receipt of assistance 90 wive', 165 children,six widows and 52 others. The average weekly expenditure was £32, but it was expectesl that the re- turn of the first contingent of the volunteers would reduce the weekly expenditure by about £5 per week.oo the other hand there was likely to be a further demand upon the fund owing to the embodiment of militia battalions to relieve others in South Africa. During the war four volunteers hid died in South Africa, and nine others, reservists or militia, had also Met their death. Then they had had a large number invalided home. They would see that the whole of the expenditure in the administration of the fund consisted in the printing, advertising and pos age charges. The distribution of the fend had been done entirely by members of the Cor- poration staff, after investigation in all the cases. No charge whatever had been incurred in connection with the administration of this large amount of money Every case had been considered on its merits,and he was extremely pleased to say that In only two cases had the committee been compelled to take dras'ic means to en- sure euod conduct on the part of recipients of the fund. The School Girls Fund had been used up to now for several matters not directly associated with the fund but indirectly associated, and in connection with which they did not want to make special appeals for help. They exnected to reduce their weekly expenditure to probably £3os week when the Volunteers who were now on the way home, had returned. If they could get £3O per week guaranteed as long as the war lasts it would tide them over their difficulties. He would like to say how *splendidly the works of the town had done. It had not only been praiseworthy but gratifying in every possible sense and if the works would undertaike some portion of this £3O weekly it ought not to be difficult to raise it. He thought it would be preferable to appeal for a weekly amount as long as the war lasts instead of appealing for a lump sum, and each works in the town could then subscribe a portion of the weekly sum re- quired. He did not suggest for a moment that the works should subscrible the whole of it, for there were numerous individual subscribers who were willing to contribute; ( Applause.) Colonel RIDGWAY hoped the Mayor's suggestion would be adopted. He thought a circular might be sent to the works of the town showing how the money had been distributed. He felt sure that the sum required would be forthcoming. £3O a week did not seem much for a town of 60,000 inhabitants to raise, and he thought Warrington would not be behindhand in caring for the wives-and families of those who were doing their duty in South Africa. He should be very glad to subscribe sum. (Hear, hear.) Mr T H COOK said the report of the Mayor was very satisfactory and the amount of money required he con- sidered very small indeed. The firm be represented (Messrs Reynolds's) would do.its share. He found that more money:was obtained in the works when individual application was made to the men. They seemed to close -their eyes when passing the box. (Laughter.) He bad got a good deal more by taking the box to the men. Mr DALLIW remarked that at Mr Davenport's works the boys gave a penny, the labourers twopence and the tradesmen threepence. The subscriptions were dividel between the Infirmary and the War Fund.
1 tfieL
Alderman FAIRCLOLTOII thought each works should be asked to subscribe a certain sum weekly, as long as the war lasts. _
Mr T H Con seconded.

The resolution was unanimously carried. The MAYOR thanked those present for the sympathy they had shown in the movement. The duty devolving upon them in this matter was practically a sacred duty and he (the Mayor) looked upon it in that Sense. When men wont out to maintain inviolate the integrity of the empire, and were willing to offer life and limb, while we staved at home, it was a very little thing for us to see that the wives and children did not suffer. They had doubtless read of cases years ago when men returned from the Crimea they found their wives and families in the Workhouse. He was glad to think that a better state of feeling existed and so far as they in Warrington knew, no woman or child had had to go to the parish for relief when the breadwinner was fight- ing for the country thousands of miles away. (Applause). The meeting concluded with an acknowledgment of the tdayor'.l serviced.

People universally have faith in the curative and nourishiogproperties of cod-liver oil, but ills some- times hard to convince them that they can take it and digest it. A little girl in the North of London had been very delicate from birth, and her parents wanted her to have the advantage of cod-liver oil. In telling about the case in a letter, they say : " 92, Drayton Park,

"London, N.: 11la-y 24 h, 1900." " Gentlemen,—Our little girl was born with a very delicate constitution, and her health has given us a great deal of trouble. We thought if we could get:her to take cod-liver oil it would do her:good,and we decided to try it. but we found that the child simply could act take it; it seemed too heavy for her to digest. Finally, it occurred to us to try Scota's Emulsion. and the results have been really remarkable. Our child took Scott's Emulsion readily, and digested it without any difficulty, the result being one healthy and steady progress in her health, No parents could desire more, and no money could brim: better results. It is with pleasure that we send you this testimonial.—Yours faithfully, "(Signed) GEII2OE AND F. A. Mourn:is."
CARRIAGE LAMP MAKER. EDWARD BINNION, 4, AUDLEY STREET, LONDON ROAD, LIVERPOOL.

One would scarcely imagine that Scott's Emulsion is really cod-liver oil. The taste of the cil is die- euised and the preparation has a very agreeable flavour, children especially being fond of it. But it is in the form of the oil that Cie greatest advantage of Scott's Emulsion really rests. The stomach has little or nothing to do with it. and ab3orption takes place without unnecessary digestive cffort. bcott's Emulsion has quite taken the place of ether forms of cod-liver oil in the treatment of chronic ailments and disease. Practical demonstra- tions of the readiness with which it is taken and the benefits it affords have convinced the medical pro- fession of its superiority. If you want the most economical and most effectual form ot cod-liver oil, you should certainly take the genuine Scott's Emul- sion.

Cheshire County Council Scholarships. At the meeting of toe Technical Instruction Com- mittee, held on Friday last, the results of the examiaation for scholarships to enable pupils from elementsry schools to proceed to secondary school... were presented. It appears that citut of the 262 candidates who sat for the examination no less than 55 or 21 per cent obtained the requisite number of marks,i.e , 70 per cent of the whole, to qualify for a scholarship. The 34 scholarships vacant were awarded to the following.—James Harnaman, Alvan:ley School ; Gertrude Curzon, Winning- ton Park School ; Frank B Moore, Winning- ton Park School ; John Rathbotie, Winning.. ton Park School; John W Marsh, Township school, Sale; Ernest Barlow, Weaver Navigation School, North wich ; Joseph H Adams, Board school, Coppenh all. Vernon Edge, St. George's School, Hyde ; Varion Bennett Stubbs, Technical School, Winsford ; David Robinson, National School, Whar- ton ; lords Owen, Victoria Board School, Runcorn ; Christina it Thomas, Edles,on-road School, Crewe ; Amy Eleanor Hale, Poulton-road Board School, Seacombe ; John Smeath Thomas, Hargrave School ; Jonn Edward Holland, Weaver Navigation School, Northwich ; James H R Burn, Victoria- road Board School, Runcorn George Hankey, Weaver Navigation School, Northwich ; Arthur Williamson, Brunner School, Barnton ; Ethel Barker, Winniugton Fark School ; Arthur Wesdall, National School, Witton; Harry North, Board School Coppenhall ; Kathleen Maloney, Flowery Field Schools, Hyde ; William H E Crosland, Township Schools, Sale ; John Alexandra Thompson, Poulton- road Board Schools. Seacombe; John Wilde, Flowery Field School, Hyde ; Frank N Billington, Seamows Moss School ; Samuel A Shams, Ashton Hayes School ; Albert Dutton, Tilstone Sehool,Tarporley; Harold James Davies, Waverton School ; Sydney Walker. div.head: WARRINGTON AUDITORS AND ALDERMEN.
div.p: WARRINGTON AUDITORS AND ALDERMEN.
Alleged Trading with the Corporation.
Investigation Committee Appointed.

The Borough Auditors have presented their report on tbo Warrington Cprporation Accounts for the , year ending March 31st, 1901. We are not in a position to give our, readers a copy of the report, but we understand that the auditors after report- ing that the accounts were found to be correct,pro- ceed to allegs that they find that three members of the Corporation have been interested in certain transactions with the Corporation. To particularice we may state that the three members alluded to are Alderman Shaw Green (chairman of the Finance and Estate Committee) ; Alderman Sutton (chair- man of the Street Improvement Committee and the Health Committee); Alderman Fran- comb (chairman of the Water Committee). With reference to the first named gentle- man, we understand that the auditors call attention to a small account of his for services rendered in a professional capacity in connection with negotiations for the transfer of land. Attention is also called by the auditors to an account presented by a son of Mr Alderman Sutton for services as auctioneer in connection with the sale of Corporation property, &c. With regard to Alderman Francomb, the auditors refer to certain trading transactions with the Corporation which require explanation,

A meeting of the Gene ral Purposes Committee was held at the Town Hall, on Friday, owing to the holidays. The proceedings were, of course private but we learn that the auditors report was presented and that a discussion took place with respect to its contents, and explanations given respecting the matters men- tioned in the report. Ultimately a small commit- tee was appointed to investigate the matter and to report to the committee. Needless to say the re- port will be,awaited with keen interest,.

div.head: LOCAL AMBULANCE BRIGADE. Complimented. by the Inspector.
div.p: THE LOCAL AMBULANCE BRIGADE. Complimented. by the Inspector.

The Warrington Corps of the St. John Ambulance Brigade paraded at the Gymnasium on Thursday last week, for the annual inspection, which was made by Assistant Commissioner Derham (Cnief Constable of Blackpool), There were present :—Captain G Crosfield, Chief Superintendent, Captain Waring, Superintendent Baldry and all the other officers of the corps. Mr Der- ham asked Superintendent Baldry to put them through a series of mpyements in company drill and stretcher work, after which he examined them in theory and first aid.

At the close of the inspection Mr Derham mid it gave him great plea.ure to testify to the efficiency of the corps. The work done that evening had been done well, and reflected great credit on the officers. There had been a great advance since last inspection, and in his report to headquarters he would be able after what he bad seen to speak very highly of them. Superintendent BALDRY replyi,g said it was very gratifying to him and the officers, non-commission officers and men, to know that they had given satisfac- tion but it was doubly gratifying to him as they had been compelled to mlinquish Brigade work for the last three months in order to run an association class owing to there being none formed anywhere else. In answer to a circular which he sent to manufacturing firms in town asking for men to join a class, 80 men had come , forward of whom 50 had qualified and had been exam- ined a week ago, when only three failed to obtain the certificate. Nearly 30 of this new class had now joined the Brigade. With reference to last inspection be said it took place at a time when their best men and most of the officers were engaged in South Africa but most of thesq had now returned as might be seen at a , glance along the ranks. The men were all wearing the South African War ribbon for the first time.

Mr DERHAM questioned Messrs Buckley and Manseur about their services and was very pleased to hear they had been out so long and that without exception the men had all brought good testimonials bick from doctors under whom they had served. Cotasin a ILSAOIIIPIELD said beswould like to take the opportunity which had been denied him before to thank the men of the Corps for the handsome present which they had made him on his departure for South Africa. Ele was also pleased to learn that out of the Corps of about 56 no less thin 17 had been out to South tkfrica. The Corps then broke no for ths summer months and will re-assemble the first Tnurstiay in October.

NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.

Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases smd their names and addresses to the Editor. Matter; intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and sent in, if possible, not latter than Thursday. Correspundents are strongly advisld to write briefly. A short letter has much greater chance of insertion than a long one. We cannot under ordinary circumatances under-
ta'PV).-re-t-urn :;he mAnuscriPts Watch are not used.
Municipal Election Compromises and Corporation Contracts.

Sir,-1 venture to think that these subjects should be discussed without beat and without the suggestion of improper motives on the part of those who desire to see the reputation of Warrington and its Council restored. It must be patent to all that the gocd name of the town has been serious'y damaged by the way in which the late Corporation Water Bill was promoted, and by the way in which recent Municipal elections have been "arranged," as also by the alleged heavy contracting direct and indirect, of many members of the Town Coined ith the Corporation. If, as is claimed, the arrangement of elections without any reference to the wishes of the general electorate is ter the advantage of the town, and if, as is claimed, the hands of the mem- bers of the Corporation are absolutely clean in regard to the alleged contracting with the Corporation, it is surely the duty of those responsible for the " compact "and of the members of the Council respectively to come forward and provs their positions in thelinterests of the town,and 132": r especially of themselves and of their officials At Man- chester,at Salford, at Bolton and at other places for only ght"contracting" irregularities(as ccmpared with those alleged against Warrington) many members have had to resign, or have resigned their seats. Is it unreasonable to suggest that if in connection with the Corporations named, Allermen and Councillors have" bowed to the storm" for merely "looking over the hedge" it is incom• prehensible that at Warrington where relatively speak- ing "the horse has been stolen" there has not bees found in the.. Council one man who has as yet had the courage to rise to the occasion and stand forward for the hetiour of the town and of public morality! Se far those who have called attention to these grave matters have done so openly, and in their own names (I refer to Mr Kenyon, Mr Flanagan, Mr Pemberton, and last but not least Mr Edwin Woods). This is satis- factory, and it those who differ from these gentlemen will follow suit, avoiding personal imputations, ad the threatening of legal procesdings, adhering simply to the issues, I see nothing but public advantage horn full ventilation ;indeed,it seems to me that nothing less than the fullest investigation will now avail.—Yours faith- f Warrington 30h May, 1901
JAMES DODDS.

Sir,—On reading the second lettet by " Maxim " in your issue of last Saturday I thought be might have done worse,but was sorry he had not done better. S-me people seem to think "Maxim" may possibly be a gen- tleman who occupies a responsible public position. If that be so, I would ask, are all his remarks worthy of his position, or do they when be is cairn and happy =Pet with his owa approval. It seems to me that "Maxim" and myself diff •r in reference to the me thods that are justifiable and ought to be adopted in public Life. I think that the unfettered liberty and uncor- rupted vote of the ratepayer is of far grrater Importance than the election of any individuals to the Council, and I think that a combination of the two political parties is an interference with that liberty, and tends to corrupt that vote. Under such conditions a man may be elected for a Ward who at a fairly contes- ted election the ratepayers would not have returned. The exorcise of liberty by the ratepayers and councillors Is the best safeguard of the purity of the Corner idols. this I think we bolieve that liberty is so very sacred that we have been permitted to sin rather than be deprived of it. If this be so how awful the p-eaumption, how terrible the wrong to interfere with another's freedom. Let us avoid anything approaching tyranny, coercion or intimidaticn for they are the climax of unselfishness, the ultimate of conceit. If " Maxim "is a gentleman bolaing a public position, and will servo the pubri,l unselfishly to the best of his abdity, I shall, when I know it, feel grateful to him.—Yours

div.head: S. KENYON.
div.p: S. KENYON.

Sir,—! am personally indebted to your correspondent Mr Marsh (as I feel sure all your readers are) for his interesting genealogical contribution. The family history of all our great men, including, Mr Edwin Woods is of importancs and should be preserved amongst the tradi- tions of our town. Mr Marsh might (if he is not too Modest) tell'us a little bit more about himself, as! am at prevnt in some doubt as to his identity. As to the queatiou at issue, will Mr Marsh tell us when the two political parties did not govern the municipal elections I speak of the past 20 years and say that for the whole period the council has been practically elected on politi- cal lines and the only diffArr nce between the position of affairs to-day and formerly is the fact that instead of wasting money and enerzy in fighting Wards which are distinctly Conservative or Liberal, the two parties have accepted the position relatively and done their utmost to bring out their best men for the various Wards. Because they agreed to support each other's candidates against the factious opposition of the Giughs or Cliffes cf the town, certain people have unhesitatingly made charges against the two political parties and their leaders of a most foul and calumnious charac'er. Is it likely that gentlemen of the standing and position of Mr John White and Mr John Cioofield would lend themselves to any scheme, which was intended to be or could possibly be carried out for the 1:orsonal advantage of a few men on either side, or at the expense of the whole com- munity. The suggestions of corruption and self-interest which have been made by certain people are as unfoun- ded as they are Infamous. It is vsry easy to attack a body coldorate in its collective capacity, because it can- not see its calumniators, but these cowardly scribes are particularly careful not to make specific charges against individuals which might involve the authors of such charges in the inconvenient and expensive process of litigation. A development in this direction would be interesting, and is by no means improbable.—Yours, MAXIM,

div.head: CASTNER KELLNER ALKALI COMPANY.
div.p: CASTNER KELLNER ALKALI COMPANY.
Bleaching Powder. 'Slump"

Mr Will:am Mather, M.P., the chairman of the 'Castner Kellner Alkali Company. presided at the general meeting in London, on Thursday, In moving the adoption of the report he ref wed to the falling off in profits which prevented the directors from paying the usual dividend the Company had paid since its com- mencement of work. Be was glad to say the reasons for the present position were of is simple character. Aftes alluding ta the absorption by the Kellner Company of the Aluminium Company he said in dealing with the gain of their reduced earnings, that during the past year the price of coal and other raw material—but coal chiefly—had made a difference of £ll,OOO in thiir profits. But not- withstanding this in the month of October last tho directors considered themselves justified in paying an interim dividend of 8 per cent per annum. They were in their second quarter of the year, and the directors were anticipating that the demand for bleaching powder, which was their la-gest product, would continue as active during the second as during the first half of the year, and their forward prospects were such that the directors felt sure at the end of the year they would be able to place before the shareholders the same satis- factory balance Sheet they bad done in previous years. Moreover, in the month of December they were selling a larger quantity of this bleaching ptwder than ever before, and at the end of the month prices incremed considerably. But in the first three months of the present year a very extraordinary change took place— almost an eclipse in the trade,—and notwithstanding that the prices were higher, there was almost a stag,na- tion in the demand for bleaching powder, which had continued up to the present time. They were not able to diminish the product and so they had gone on in- Craasinz stock. To that chiefly he attributed the unex- pected conclusion of the year's trading. The other pro- duct which they manufactured was caustic soda, which Stfll maintained its high place in the market. They were not able to diminish the output of bleaching powder without also diminishing that of soda because both were made from the same raw material, The transfer of the aluminium works from Oldbury to Weston Point was a Vesy considerable undertaking, which had now been successfully carried out. The report, which recommended a dividend at the rate of 5 per cent. per annum, was adopted. • CRICKET.

div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS.
Sharp Fighting in the
T ran svaal.
30 British Killed, 58 Wounded.

On May 22, 23, 24,snd 25 there was sharp figthing probably with the Boer rear-guard between Stander- ton and Bethel a )distance of thirty-six miles), in which the British had an officer and five men killed and twenty four men wounded. Acting-Chaplain Tobias,attached to the Munster Fusiliers,was severely wounded. At Bethel on May 23 and 24. two men were killed and four wounded. Fifteen men were wounded at Waitpoortj near Potchefstroom on May 23, and at Ventersdorp on May 23 one man was killed and seven w )unded. Two officers of the Rift.) Brigade were severely wounded at Zand River Poort (locality uncertain) on May 21. Four men of the South African Constabulary were killed at Engelbrechts Drift. on the Vaal, east of Johannesburg,on May 24.0ne man was killed and four wounded in fighting east of Kroonstad on May 20 and 22 In Cape Colony there was a fight at Doornhoek on May 13, in which six men of the District Mounted Rif! 25 were killed, Smaller actions have been fought at Harrisrnith, Vredefort-road, Smithfield, Lydenburg, Bethlehem, Jagersfontein- road, Muller's Pass, and Cradock.

The total of yesterday's casualties in action is thirty killed, fifty-eight wounded, and two missing. The deaths from diseme numbec seventy-five, while 147 officers and men are retursecl as dangerously ill.

div.head: UNITARIAN CONFERENCE.
div.p: UNITARIAN CONFERENCE.
Sir J. Brunner on Christian Courage.

The annual meeting of the British and Foreign Unitarian Association was held in London on Wednes- day, and there was a crowded attendance. Sir John T Brunner, MP. the president, occupied the chair, and was supported by the Rev 8 A Steinth al k Manchester), Rev H E Dawson (Gee Cross), Mr William Long, (War- rington), and Mr C W Jones (Liverpool), while several other Lancashire and Cneshire representatives were present. Sir JT Brunner, in moving the adoption of the report. said one part struck him with great Interest. He found there were no less than seven Japanese preachers of Unitarian Christianity. When he visited Japan,some 11 years ago, he was as:ured by more than one of their public men that the Japanese bad made up their minds that their country should not become another Kupt,and that they would not remain under the tutelation of Eurepe. They particularly wanted to get rid of what was called His convention and to manage the adminis- tration of justice. He now found that they not only managed the administration of justice themselves, but were equally responsible tor the spread of Cbristianity. He would ask those outside their body to declare agreement with them whenever they bad it in their hearts. Be often met people who in private conversation declared that they were in agreement will Unitarian principles, but could not obtain the consent of their wives. (Laughter.) Our fellow-countrymen tied shown on the batcefield a cour- age which was the admiration of the world, and he wished to encourage their own people to show as much courage in the moral and spiritual life as our soldiers had done in tbe war, which he prayed God, might soon come to an end. (Applause.) If they would show that courage on public questions in this country they could be dealt with in a way far higher than they were now. If a man would only have the courage to say he was a liberal Christian he would obtain the necessary courage to deal with public affairs as a Christian. An appeal had been submitted to him to put down a certain state of affairs in the streets of a particular district which was a shame not only to Christianity but to bnmanity. But in consequence of the training he had received he was Utterly unable to sign that petition, for be hated the system which barasaed the victim and left alone the tempter. (Applauge ) In conclusioa, the Chairman announced his intention Co resign the position of presi- dent, and be invited Mr Blake Odgers to accept that position. (Cheers). The report was adepted. Mr William Long (Warrington) moved and Mr Gros- venor Talbot (Leeds) seoonded a resolution of thanks to the President, the Council, and the executive committee and officers, which was carried. Sir John Brunner, in moving a resolution protesting against the proposal of the G wernment with regard to education, and declaring that no amendment or recon- struction of Education Acts could be just or satisfactory which failed to provide for an effective elective control in the management of schools and in the appointment of teachers, said they were entitled to press upon their fellow-countrymen the doctrine that those who paid for anything in this world were entitled to some control over that which was the pro- duct of their own money, and those who were outside the Church of England claimed a share in the manage- ment of the schools, which were carried on by means of national money. (Applause). They, therefore, claimed that there should be efficient popular control over all the elementary schoole. They claimed, too, to have a right to a share in the appointment of teachers, and that by means of public representation upon the management of each individual school. (Cheers): Lady O'Elagan (chairman of the Burnley School Board), seconded the in )tion which was carried unanim- I ously.

Fletcher Russell's Rugby Football Club. The annual meeting of the above club was held at the Pelican Ina, Buttermarkst-street on Friday, the 2lth met, Mr John W Mills presiding in the absence of Mr Bowers who was unable to attend through pressure of business. Mr W Sanders, the secretary, reported a fairly :successful season but said interest had flagged at the end of the season through the club not being in any league. Mr B Harris, the treasurer, reported that the club had just paid its way during the past season and hoped to do better in the future. B )th reports were adopted and the following offic srs ekcted for the next tw,. I re months• Secretary Mr W S inders,3,Mar- bury-street, Latchford ; Treasurer Mr J W Mills; Committee : Messrs. Bowers, _Harris, J Warburton, II Greening, It Price,T Brooks,J Davies,W Ifornsey, J Powell and J Brooks; Captain Mr J Ashurst . Sub-Captain Mr J Fuden ; Touch Judge Mr A Smith It was resolved that the club be entered in the most suitable league for the ensuing season. Votes of thanks to the retiring committee &c., concluded the business after which a convivial evening was spent, Mr B llarris, officiating at the piano, Messrs Sanders, Brooks, Lythgoe, and Lawless being the vocalists.

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY, MAY 31 1901.
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY, MAY 31 1901.
EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.
_Vta.cAN _WESLEYANS.

Special services in aid of the Vulcan Wesleyan Sunday Schools, were held on Sunday. Instructive discourses were preached by the' Rev P H Horrell, of St. Helens. Special and appropriate hymns were sung by the children, conducted by Mr James Platt, Mr W H Grundy presiding a•, the organ. Solos were given by Miss P Barr and Mr J Platt. The 11 collections amounted to .£4, ST MARY'S R.C. CHURCH.

Toe annual services in aid of toe Schools con- nected with the above church were held on Sunday The preacher for the day was the Rev Father An lraw. Rector of Sutton, who took for his text in the morning "Christian Education," and in the evening "The Good Shepherd." Special music was rendered by the choir, solos being sung by Miss Beatty, and Messrs Higham, Battersby aria Russell. A co!lection was made in aid of the school:. POLICE CASES

At he Police Buildlffigs, :Newton, on Monday be- fore Colonel Wood, Alice Baxter, of Wi,..mn was charged with being drunk and disorderly iu Earles- town on Saturday night, and was fined 10 i and costs. In default she was sent to gaol for 14 da3s. She had 24 previous convictions again;t her.— Charles Glynn. labourer, of Newton for being drunk .9t disorderly on Saturdsy:was fined 2i and costs. —At the same court on Tuesday, befo.e Colonel Wood, Matthew liazeldon, flaydock, was charged with being drunk and disorderly iu Earlestown and was fined 24 61 and costs. Taomas Woolham, for being drunk was fined 58 and cost. BAPTIST CHURCH, EARLESTOWN. The special services in connection with the anni- versary of the Sunday School connected with the above place of worship, were held in the chapel on 'Sunday. The weather being very inclement had an appreciable eff tct upon the attendance at the ser- vices, which were conducted by the Rev E K Everett, of Eccles. In the afternoons sacred can- tata entitled " The King in Z.on," was rendered by the choir and children under the conductorship of S Harvey. Miss Elarvey presided at the piano, and Mr T A Limond at the organ. The musical items were exceptionally wed rendered and much enjoyed by the large congregation present. The collections during the day amounted to over £45, in aid of the Sunday School. Wiirrr MONDAY AT ,EARLESTOWN AND. NEWTON.

Whitsuntide is not generally recognised as a holiday by the works in Narlestown and Newton but the whole of the tradespeople closed their shops during the whole of Monday and gave their assist- ants a day off. The weather being fine, and the air warm and balmy, a great number of the work- men became afflicted with the holiday mania, the consequence being that SGO men failed to put in an appearance at the Viaduct Works, at Messrs T and T Vicars, all the men were out, Messrs Slee and Co. had to close and a the Vulcan it was hardly worth while running the engines for the number of mert who turned up. The majority of the men journeyed to Manchester to visit Belle Vue. and to Old Traf- ford for the cricket match. The remainder hung about the street corners, whilst many visited the various houses of refreshment. The bowling greens were well patronised, and at Newton a couple of local cricket matches were played.. Notwithstand- ing the fact. that the whole of the Works in the dis- trict will close in August for the greater portion of a week,the men do not seem to be able to withstand the temptation of a holiday at Whitsuntide, and there is a rumour that in tuture the holidays will be taken during Whit week instead of August.

div.head: WARRINGTON
div.p: WARRINGTON

Coming Events. • We have pleaqur3 in announcing that the Rev Leonard M Isla, of New Zialand, will conduct a great temperance mistion in Warrington, commenc- ing to-morrow Sunday, the 2nd of June. Mr (sit% who is a Wesleyan minister, ranks amongst the ablest and most eloqumt advocates of this great reform, His voice, his mental abilities, his great sympathy for the downtrodden and oppressed, his great experience, extensive travels, comprehensive knowledge, and overflowing humour are all brought into requisition to convince and convert all wh hear him of the wisdom of true temperance to the individual, the family, and the nation. The mission will be continued nightly throughout the week. On week-nigta there will be a kinematograph exhibition.

Plucky Rescue by a Warrington Boy. On Sunday afternoon,a little boy named Thomas Freeth, aged three years four•months, living at 76, Longford-street, Warrington, was playing in the fields at Longford when he fell into ankey Brook which runs through the di4trict. The water of the brook jamn a dreadfully filthy coalition, and it was at considerable risk that a boy named John Dag- nail, fourteen years of age, of 56 John-street, man- aged to pull the child out of the water The child was taken home in an exhaust° I condition, as he had swallowed a quantity of the water. P.O Hewitt administered an emetic, after which Dr. Curtis was called in. The boy is now progress- ing favourably. We are informed that this is the second rescue from drowning which has been effected by the boy Dagnall.

Mr S Brighouse, county coroner, conducted an in- quiry at the Police Station, Warrington, on Wed- nesday evening, respecting the death of a builder's labourer. named William Aspary, 48 years of age, of Cherry-lane, Lymm, who die I at the Warrington Infirmary early the same morning from injuries re- ceived whilst following his employment on the previous day. Prom the evidence it appears that the deceased was engaged at the Spread Eagle Hotel where the owners, Messrs Budding- tons' Breweries, Limited, Manchester, are carrying on some extensions of the premiies. The deceased had mounted a ladder, carrying a slab of stone to form a corbel, weighing about 30lbs. and measuring 24 inches long by 10 inches wide, and was in the act of lifting it on to a scaff tld, 14 feet high, when he overbalanced himself, and both he and the s'one fell to the bottom. A witness named Percy Ardern stated that the deceased fell with his elbow on the ground with such force as to drive the wrist into his (deceased's) ribs. The stone fell clear of the deceased. James M'Carthy, f )reman, said the lad- der was fastened to the scoffold and was s'ill secure after the accident,. His opinion was that the deceased over-balance 1 himself as he was trying to " land " the stone on the scaff Ad.—Nurse Moore, of the Warrington Infirmary,depoed that the deceased died a few hours after admittance. Hs was suffer- ing from a fractured thigh and arm and internal injuries.-51r Christopher Higginbottom said Messrs Boddingtons had been carrying out this kind of work for over 20 years. and this was the first acci- dent which had occur A.—The jury returned a verdict of accidental death. div.head: ON TOUR.
div.p: ON TOUR.
A Week-end Spin of 200 Miles.

Taere are still many cyclists who have never been on tour and who are quite content to potter about in their own immediate locality. A week ago I was one of these somewhat unenlightened indivi- duals, but the glowing eulogies of a touring friend ' made me decide that a cycle-tour if only short,was absolutely necessary. So a tour for the Whitsun week-end was immediately decided upon and pre- liminaries arranged. Among the preliminaries wasl the obtaining of a co mpenion,arui fortunate'y,there was no diflimity aboot this for I knew well ivhere to find another cyclist ignorant of what touring really was and willing to give it a trial. There were three days at liberty for us to " see the world " in, or as much of it as was possible. It was a sine qua non with us that new country must be traversed entirely; we were not going t, spend precious time in cycling over roads which we knew by the inch, so to speak, and a t sur which would take us over quite 200 miles of " fields and pastures new "—to say nothing of rivers and mountains—was accord- ingly mapped out. The first part of the journey Was to be by train—yes, train —as far as Ruabon —where the bricks come from. Saturday moraine saw us therefore on board the 8 17 train frem Bank Q Lay Station, and a little over an hour later we were at our starting-point proper. The fact that we were able t 3 free-wheel down from Ruabon S atiou to the high-road which was to lead us out into the unknown seemed a good omen and we I cheerfully took it as such. ifence, onward to Chirk and Oswestry. A fast spin down into the Llan- gollen Vale was so delightful that the climb Out on the Ceirk side was not grumbled at for a moment, Tae " going" was good though the duet lay literally in furrows on the road. It was inches deep in many places, but there was not enough wind to raise it, and with tyres blown beard-hard what cared we for the dazzling carpet even though a little power may have hem lost thereby ? We were soon at Oswes- try, the heal of the Cambrian Rail way System, and an interesting town to boot. Oswestry contests with Winwick the local fame of King: eawald's martyrdom which occurred, here or elsewhere, in the year 6-12. That's rather a long time ago,and it would not ben- efit King Oswald or anybody else very much if the ' claim of either place was proved to be incontestable. Thera are plenty of:other points of attraction about Oswestry, which shows traces of having been at one time a considerable British encampment, but We could not stay to examine them. Tempus was fuyitrng and our itinerary ebowed that we had plenty before us for that day. His Glorious Majesty of the Heavens had, by now, got full steam up and we were getting it hot, so the purchase of a white sun-hat each seemed, and proved, wise. Continuine the journey,our next place of interest was Llanymy- nech famous as an anglers' resort, and a favourite rendezvous of Warrington pliers of the supple rod. We saw no faces we knew, however, and the place had a sleepy air about it quite , in keep'ng with the atmosphere and the don't-care- whether-1-get-there-or-not behaviour of the stream., Thera is not much water between the banks, but a few minutes pause on the bridge convinced us that the fishermen had something to fish for. The toilet pools within sight all had their finny deniz mils glid- ing about as though eager tor the succulent warm or fly offered by the angler. *lt was the same when- ever we crossed a stream small or great,—there were the fish waiting to be caught. Welshpool was the next calling place after leaving L'anymynech, and on the way we obtained a fine view of th Breidden Hills, whose bold outline showed through the heat-haze, on our left. We noticed hereabouts that the mile-stones and sign-posts, with which Wales is liberally pro- vided, neatly all dropped the " Welsh" and informed us every 1760 yards that it was " Pool" we were getting nearer and nearer to. By and by we get there feeling warm, dusty, very much thirsty, and not a little hungry. The needs of the inner man were promptly attended to at a commodious hostelry on the left of the main street A short interval was allowed to lapse after lunch, and then on we went down the lovely Severn Valley. Toe roads were still dusty but were noticeably improving in this respect as regions where traffic was less abundant were reached. We were now travelling straight towards the moun- tains and at Berriew were well within their com- pass. The road woene on and on round thickly wooded hills and through leafy avenues, always keeping in the valley bottom in a way very accept- table to us wheelmen. The surface was remark- ably level, though the country was so mountainous, and there was ne'er a hill that pre• sented the slightest difficulty to surmount without a dismount. Soon we were entering Newtowno which does not belie its name, and which had a rather too businesslike air to be as charming as other places we passed through. The Price Jones establishment was obtrusive.and we knew we were in the centre of the Welsh flannel and wool indus- try. Thirteen and a half miles further on is the market-town of Llanidloes, which was just as busy as Newtown but vastly more old-fashioned and less commercial-looking. There seemed to be quite a gathering of the clans, for the country-folk were present in large numbers, and many of them jabber- ing away in Welsh. In the streets you saw the most antique coster-barrowe and Stalls, all doing a thriv- ing trade Here it was tucuinbent upon us to have tea,and we gave the Welsh an instructive lesson in English appetites. There is a climb up from Llan- idloes, where we said good-bye to the Severn, and the first two miles involved a certain amount of collar-work. Every band in the road disclosed another up-gradieut, and at last when our tempera- ture seemed a long way ahead of fever-heat we jibbed. Another turn, and up again, this time with added steepness. We walked it, and of course it was, the last turn and hhe last rise. At the top, a cigarette and a luxurious sprawl on a bank suited perfectly to the outline of the human fieure, were some compensation for the grind. The view, too, was charming, and overhead a joyous lark was singing away in the Cimmerian blue, or whatever the poet might like to call it. Then there ' was a steady drop down into Llangurig, at which pretty little spot we made acquaintance with the river Wye, here only tiny stream fresh from its source on lofty flYnltmnion. From Llangurig we entered on the last lap of our first day's ride, the ten miles or so into Rhavader. This stretch of road proved the finest in scenery we had so far traversed. ' The mountains become more abrupt and wilder, the road itself winding round the steep slope of Pantydwr. A hundred feet below was the Wye, wineing along a rocky gorge which must be a veritable whirlpool during storm. The rocks were washed smooth on each side ' in eloquent testimony to the raging torrent which ofttimes comes. tumbling down. At eight o'clock in the evening we entered Rhayader, alter a spin of seventy .miles, none of which could by any stretch of imagination be termed arduous riding, an 1 we were. fresh enough to feel that the dof enjoyment. Rhayader ssmall, precipitous streets, ia ay had typical been Welshoneto w entirelya white washed housets, and the usual stone bridge over the river. which at this point falls a few feet and is of considerable width The town is envie rowel by bold mountains, divided by equally bold tavine3, and is a p iradLie alike for the angler, the artist, and the pedestrian. Its lofty situation, seven hundre i feet above sea levee and close proxi- mity to the mountains renders the air singularly pure and exhilarating, quite in contrast to Llanid- loes, which struck us me being rather a close, stuffy little place. Rhayader, though only a small town, is not without a good hotel, and we found excellent accommodation at the" Lion." Our motto was the good old one of " early to bed and early to rise," bnt we only followed out the first portion of it in actual practice. It was after ten on Sunday morning before we were fairly on the way again, still following the course of the river and riding along a road splendidly shaded by trees, towards Buieth,a town very pleasnntly situated and popular as a holiday resort. Our stay here was only long enough to quaff some of the palatable cider which is so plentiful a beverage in this part of the country. From Bineth our journey was still southward, through the pretty- villages of Erwood and Boughrood. Between these two places rain commenced to fall and on arrival at the latter we seriously meditated a halt. Just here there is a bridge over the river, and at the opposite side a very formidable gateway with a toll-house alongside. On the other side of the toll-gate was the Boat Inn which invited shelter, We stood and pondered, looking first at the sky and then at the Inn, Our meditations were soon interrupted by the old lady who extracts toll from wayfarers and who came forth to inform us that we must pay 21, each to pass through the gate We declinee without thanks, particularly as the. rain seemed to he on the point of ceasing, and our way Was still along the river bank and not through the toll-gate. The oil lady was loath to lose her coppers and :remarked none too courteously :

"Well you have crossed the water and you must pay a penny each." Extortion ! and noth- ing el " We'll be hanged if we will " were our joint sentiments and off we rovle leaving the avaricious old dame in high dudgeon and with her parting Parthian shot " ) on then ; you're of no amount anyway," ringing in our ears. A run of a few more miles brought us to Three C,clis Junction our furthest point south, the arrival at which we celebrated by taking lunch. From here we turned north-east and pedalled steadily along through such quaint old places as May, Whitney Bridge. Willersley and Weobley to Dilwyn. Across country as were now travelling the nail was none too evy,and the gradients of that type which make you ashamed to get off and walk and yet take it out of you by the time you have ridden to the top. There was something thundery about the atmosphere too, laud we were none too vigorous when Dilwyn was reached. People here were just thinking of going to Church, but we managed to get tea for all that, and never did I for one feel more in want of "cup that cheers," &c. Thera bad been an odd shower or two during the afternoon, but not enough to delay us appreciably. It was only some six miles to Leominster from Dilwyn and we calculated on resoling that place at least before the lowering clouds overhead brake. The meal refreshed as and we got along well to within two miles of the town when the storm came on and macintosh capes had to be unstrapped. Thus accoutred we looked genuine tourists when we passed through the street of Leominster (" Lemster" colloquially). The rain was now persistent and the deesion to cover the remaining ten miles into Ludlow was soon come to when we found that Sunday evening trains were not unheard of things in that I locality. At Ludlow it was fine again and though the Owe was pretty full, mine host of the Ex- change was able and willing to "take us in and do for us." Ludlow is indeed a charming old town, much like Chester, only far less modernised. The river Tame here is very beautiful, and the view of the surrounding hills from the tower of the fine old Castle is not to be easily surpassed. They don't w ste gas in Ludlow streets when there is a chance of the moon appearing, so that we found the place shrouded in semi-gloom,rather in keeping with the air of belonging to the middle-ays which the town has. There is a clock on Ludlow Church which possesses qualities of a " striking " descrip- tion, and if you had slept just below it as we did you would not be inclined to doubt the assertion Every four hours, in addition to indicating the time, the clock plays a tune for the benefit of all within hearing. We heard it at midnight when, after chiming twelve very melodiously, it wandered off into the strains of " See the conquerhig hero comes" without variation 4, but repeated four times. The same thing recurred at four in the morning— when we were, fortunately, quite oblivious —and every four hours until midnight again, when the tune changes.. The clock's repertoire includes"flome sweet home " and "Annie Rooney " that we know of, and also, perhaps, "Soldiers of the Queen," if echoe 3 of that impressive chant have yet reached Ludlow. In the morning our trusty steeds were as ready as their masters, and after a prowl nand the historic castle ruins where the jackdaws do congre- gate, we were off once more and bowling along the magnificent road:to Church Stretton. The previous night's shower had made the " going " perfect and the sun shone once more so that our hearts were as light as those of the birds which carolled so cheer- fully in the trees. From Ludlow to Church Stretton is a splendi l run possessing I scenic atfractions which we had not seen surpassed during the whole journey, while the road itself bore out the high reputa- tion of Shropshire for road-making. And what a fine drop it is from Church Stratton to Shrewsbury! We free-wheeled the whole of the first five miles and felt that this was indeed cycling. Once at Shrewsbury and it seemed that home was not very far off,thougt there was still some very stiff riding to be done through VVem to Whitchurch. Here we made our last stay, partook once more of tea, and set off in time to catch the 8-5 express from Crewe to Warrington. As in starting we thought highly of the advantage of doing the last 20 odd miles by rail instead of road. Somehow it seems to me to take a lot of the cream off a long ride if you have to finish up on the same old roads you have ridden over scores of times. Anyhow the train seemed a very comfortable and expeditious way of travelling after cycling 200 miles in three days, and m oreover it landed us at "good old Warrington" feeling absolutely "fit" and quite convinced that, given the excellent weather we had enjoyed, touring awheel was as pleasant a way of spending a holiday as any we had tried. Our first will not, we hope, be our last tour.

div.head: SAD DRONNING FATALITY.
div.p: SAD DRONNING FATALITY.
A warrington Pork Butcher Found in the Ship Canal.

As some workmen at Stockton Heath were walk- ing near the Ship Canal early on Tuesday m-irning, they saw 11 iating in the water what appeared to them to be the body of a child. Information was given to the bridgeman at Twenty-Step Bridge and he and Police Constable Tarte succeeded in bring- ing the body to the bank. It was found to be the body of a MEM about 40 years of age,lengtb Eat Tin, complexion fresh,hair dark,moustache sandy,other- wise clean shaven, full raund features, somewhat stout build, dressed in black worsted coat, vest and trot** of grey plaid, white turn down collar and front, grey and red striped shirt, blue woollen stockings. A watch with heavy silver chain, and Queen Anne shilling as a pendant were found on toe boiy In the packets were some cards bearing the following name "William Mattock, Boat House Inn, Agden Bridge, Altrincham." ' Mr Dob.on conducted an inquiry at the Red Lion Inn, Stackton Heath, on Thursday morning. Charlotte Shadwell was the first witness called and stated that the deceased was her husband. They lived at 26, Pinners Brow Warrington. He was a pork butcher by trade and was 40 years of age. He was at work all day on Tuesday last, he being employed by Mr J Bayley Isaac. He came home about five o'clock and had his tea. Towards seven o'clock he went out and returned home about ten minutes to eleven. At the time he was under the influence of drink. Ste gave him his supper and whilst she was standing at the front door, de- ceased suddenly left by the back way. She did not see him alive again, fla had been in regular work but for the last few days he had been low spirited. She did not know the cause. If had never given any reason to think that he would take away his life.

John Thorass Goolliffe, of I, WiLlerspiol-terrace, Wilderspool, said be w tie bridgeman at Twenty Step Bridge. He received information from some workmen about six a in on the previous day that there was a body in the canal floating under the swing bridge. Lie found that was ea, and inf u.meti the police. He then recovered the body. It was fully dressed, the cap only being missing. Captain Waring lc tormed the jary that a cap was found near the linutsford-road swing bridge, and he gave instructions for it to be sent to the Stockton Heath police. _
Sergeant Bourne produced the cap and said the deceased's wife stated that it belonged to the deceased.

Captain Waring said the deceased would have to climb over the rails near the bridge in order to get to the p 1 ice where the cap was found. Tarte stationed at Sockton Heath stated that he received informatio:i from the last witness that there was a body in the Ship Canal and he assisted to recover it and to remove it to the Red Lion Inn. There were no marks of violence on the body but there was a slight bruise on the nose. He searched the clothing and found a silver lever watch, a silver albert chain, but no money. There were also three cards in the pockets bearing the address : William Mattock, Boat House Inn, Agien Bridge, Altrincham• He received a cloth cap that morning from the bridgeman at the Knutsford-road bridge.and learned that it belonged to the decease,l.
Mrs Shadwell was recalled and identified tho cap as being that of her husband's. He was wearing it en Tuesday night. The jury returned a verd'ct of " Fiund Drowned."

div.head: ECHOES OF THE CENSUS. A Pleasant wind up to the Work in Warrington.
div.p: ECHOES OF THE CENSUS. A Pleasant wind up to the Work in Warrington.
Presentation to the Registrar.

Those gentle.nen who undertook the exacting,and in many cases,arduous duties of enumerators in the recent census, had a most agreeable duty to per- form on Monday evening, namely to receive the remuneration for their services. As our readers will doubtless have concluded by this, taking the census is no light task, and it was a relief to all concerned, when the work at 'A ar- rington was ea' isfactorily completed. The difficul- ties which beset the enumerators, however, might have been much more numerous, had it not been for the willingness of the genial Registrar (Mr W H Harrison) to render them any possible assistance. This fact was forcibly demon- strated on Monday evening, when, after receiv- ing the monetary reward for their services, the entunerators assembled for the purpose of presenting Mr Hirrison with somo recognition of the esteem in which he is held by them. The gathering took place in the Druids' Ball, Sankey- street, Mr Edwin Plinston occupying the chair. Most if not all the enumerators were present, the proceedings taking the form of a smoking concert. A capital programme had been arranged, aid the artistes acquitted themselves very creditably. The following gentlemen took part: Messrs Ankland,G Parr, P Woollacott. Healing, P Delaney,John Haul- son, C H Hoult, and Babbitt. All the items were well received, special praise teing due to Mr Aukland for his rendition of " The BAndolero." This song so viewed the audience that they demanded an encore, and Mr Aukland responded with the ever-popular" Boys of the old brigade." A humor- ous recitation by Mr Delaney created roars of laughter. Mr G Finch and Mr B Smith supplied the pianoforte accompaniments. Shortly after the commencement of the concert

IThe CHAIRAIAN explained that be occupied that posi- tion at the request of the committee appointed to carry out" the presentation. The duties they had had to per- form as enumerators had been brought to a very happy climax, and they bad assembled to perform the pleasantest part of their duty, and that was to give a receipt for their money. (Laughter). Right through the census, up till that evening, chey had received from Mr Harrison the utmost courtesy. He had been as-kind as possible t every enumerator, and now they had met to enjoy themselves at a convivial meeting. He sup- pose° the object for which they had met was no longer a secret to Mr Harrison and he was pleased to find so many present to show in a tangible form the esteem entertained for Mr Harrison. This was the first time that he (the chairman) had met him in the position of enumerator but he bad bad a very long acquaintance with him and had always found him to be a gentleman In every respect. He had the utmost pleasure in taking part in that night's proceedings, not only to meet the other enumerators but also to meet Mr Harrison. At a later stage of the meeting he would have something further to sayt Several other songs having been rendered, The CHAIRMAN expressed how sincerely he agreed with the presentation to Mr Harrison .The committee appointed to carry it out simply wished to make a small presenta- tion to Mr Harrison as a memento ,of the good feeling which existed between the enumeratsrs and himself. They, did not de ire to give him an elaborate present, as they knew that Mr Harrison would not wish them to do so, but j Ist a small token of their fegard for him and also a Memento ot the first cenPul in the new century. (Applause.) Mr. DRUMM then made the presentation in suitable terms. He said that the enumerators wished to identify themselves with the new century, and the only way to do so was to a.k Mr Harrison's acc...ptance ot a little testimonial. They asked him to ac .r pt of an illumin- ated address and a harometer, as they conveyed with them the best wishes of the staff which bad worked under his instructions. He trusted he would long be spared—he was going to say to see the taking of many eensusea—to meet them under such pleasant circum• 571,1C89. The enumerators hoped their work had ben done to the satisfaction of the Registrar and the ltgiqtrar-General. Mr fißtaffekt then handed to Mr Harrison a beautiful framed illuminated address and a handsome aneroid barometer. The address had been illuminated and en- graved by Mr T Sargeant, of Marshhouse-lane, who had executed the work most taetsfully. The text of the address was as follows :—"Presented to Mr William H Harrison, registrar, together with an aneroid barometer as a token of esteem, and as a memento of the first cen- sus of the 20th century, by the enumerators associated with ha in taking the census for the County Borough of Warriogton in the year 1901 " Appended were the names of fifty six enumerators, the following being the members of the committee.—John Clayton, Peter De- laney, C U Houle, Edwin Plinston, Alfred Taylor, and the bon secretary and treasurer, George William Rigby. Messrs Edstance and Company had suoptied the barc na- star which bore the following inscription :—"County Borough of Warrington, 1901. Presented to Mr W H Harrison, registrar, as a memento of the first census in inthe 20th century by the enurnerators,May 14.th,1901." Councillor Hun said he had great pleasure in bear- ing his testimony to Mr Harrison's work. It reflected great credit upon him and upon his judgment in having selected such an intelligent body ot men to act as his enumerators. (Laughter.) Mr Harrison was a most intimate friend of his, and he knew from him that the services of the enumerators were appreciated. Not only was Mr Harrison a personal friond,but he (the speaker) bad been in some manner connected with his family a long time before he came to Warrington, which made the presentation all the more gratifying to him (Mr Hulse). Since the Registration Act of 1837 came into force—the year of the accession of the late Queen to the Throne—the registrarship had been in the Harrison family for three generations, arid it was a curious coin- cidence that the last census should have been taken at the time the new King ascended the Throne. He hoped all present would live to see the next census taken if they did not take part in the work of enumeration, and that Mr rlarrison would live long to appreciate the kindly feeling which existed between himself and the enumerators. Mr JOHN CLAYTON thoroughly endorsed all the previous speak ,es had said in regard to Mr flarrison,and said that he, too, had been closely associated with him. He had known him since be came to Warrington and had in some respects regarded him as his " guide, philosopher and friend." (Applause.) He had always found him to be courteous and obliging and ready to supply any information. Mr Hammon, who had a most hearty reception,said he rose with a very full heart as they could easily understand He did not know why he had been thought deserving of such a magnificent testimony of their good fellowship. They all knew that the work which had been done had been both pleasant and laborious. That had been the

hit I census he had had to deal with, but it had n'tl always been his good luck to have got hold of such ag excellent body of gentlemen to act as enumerators. The. work had been thoroughly well done. He was 11°' speaking on his own behalf, but on bahah of ego' enumerator. Great pains were taken to go through th: hooka. It took about a fortnight, and they minutely examined, along with the schedules and forth, and compared, and he bad found that an exceed' ingly easy work The enumeration was so well doee,f and many of the bloke were a perfect picture to losi, at. Ho was not ashamed of the Somerset 130058 authorities examining Warrington fmnsus books, for. 00 the whole, the work could not have been better done', With regale the testimonial, he felt deeply grate to all present. It was not the intrinsic value of .the presents for which he felt grateful, but the good feehrig which had been extended to him on that occasion. Be had only done what had been his duty, and what infer niatien he had given had been givan with the greate!O pleasure with the object of assisting tbe enumeratorelo their difficult task. He accipted the gifts with a fun heart, and trusted he would be spared to look upcal them for many years to come. He would certainly re; member the kind faces of the enumerators and the go°' work they had helped him to do. (Applause). file remainder of the evening was spent convivially.
